0.title: The God Who Redeems: The Book of Exodus
0.overview:
Exodus is the great drama of redemption. If Genesis tells us how the world was made and how it fell, Exodus tells us how God comes down to rescue a people for himself. Here the God who walked in Eden, who called Abraham, who promised a multitude, now bends the heavens and bares his arm. He hears groaning. He remembers covenant. He descends in fire. "I have surely seen the affliction of my people," he says, "and I have come down to deliver them" (Ex. 3:7-8). That single sentence is the gospel in seed form: a holy God who sees, who hears, who remembers, and who comes down.

The book unfolds in three great movements. First, redemption accomplished (chs. 1-18): Israel groans in Egypt, Moses is raised up, the plagues fall, the Passover lamb is slain, and the people pass through the sea from death to life. Second, the covenant given (chs. 19-24): at Sinai the redeemed people receive the law, not as a ladder to climb to God but as the shape of life with the God who has already saved them. Third, the presence secured (chs. 25-40): the tabernacle is commanded, the golden calf nearly undoes everything, mercy triumphs, and at last the glory of the LORD fills the tent. The book that opens with a people enslaved in a foreign land ends with God himself dwelling in their midst.

Exodus is relentlessly about God. Israel does almost nothing to save itself; it cries out, it trembles, it grumbles, it sins. Salvation is the LORD's from beginning to end. As R.C. Sproul loved to insist, the central issue of Exodus is the character of God — his holiness, his faithfulness, his sovereignty, his steadfast love. When Moses asks to see his glory, God answers by proclaiming his name: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness" (34:6). That is the heartbeat of the book.

And every page points to Christ. The Passover lamb without blemish is fulfilled when Paul writes, "Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed" (1 Cor. 5:7). The Red Sea is our baptism (1 Cor. 10:2); the manna is the bread of life (John 6); the rock struck in the desert is Christ (1 Cor. 10:4); the tabernacle anticipates the Word made flesh who "tabernacled among us" (John 1:14). Moses, the mediator who stands in the breach and offers his own life for the people, is a shadow of the one Mediator who actually gave his. To read Exodus rightly is to be led, step by step, out of bondage and up the mountain, until we see that the God who redeems is the God who in Jesus Christ came down to redeem us forever.

1.title: A People Multiplied in the Furnace
1.text: <sup>7</sup>But the people of Israel were fruitful and increased greatly; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them. <sup>8</sup>Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph. <sup>12</sup>But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and the more they spread abroad. <sup>17</sup>But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live.
1.overview:
Exodus opens by tying itself back to Genesis: the names of the sons of Israel who came down to Egypt. The family of seventy has become a people. The command of Eden — "be fruitful and multiply" — and the promise to Abraham of descendants like the stars are quietly, irresistibly being fulfilled, even in a foreign land, even under the lash.

Then comes the ominous sentence: "there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph." The world turns. The favored guests become hated slaves. Pharaoh launches the first program of genocide in Scripture, and yet the more Egypt presses down, the more Israel spreads. As Alistair Begg notes, oppression cannot finally defeat the purposes of God; the bush burns but is not consumed. Into this furnace step two unlikely heroes, the Hebrew midwives Shiphrah and Puah, who fear God more than Pharaoh and so quietly defy the empire.

This chapter sets the theological stage for the whole book. God's people suffer, but God's promise advances. The growth of Israel under affliction is the first sign that a power greater than Pharaoh is at work.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The seventy who came to Egypt have become a teeming people. Exodus deliberately echoes the creation mandate and the Abrahamic promise: Israel's fruitfulness is the visible keeping of God's word.
verseByVerse.theology: God's covenant promises advance through ordinary providence — births, families, generations — long before any dramatic intervention.
verseByVerse.examples: Count the quiet faithfulness of God in the unremarkable growth of your own family, church, and years. The kingdom often advances unseen.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of Israel were fruitful and increased greatly; they multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, so that the land was filled with them.
verseByVerse.commentary: Five verbs of fruitfulness pile up: fruitful, increased, multiplied, grew, strong. Calvin observes that God multiplied them precisely when human reason would expect them to dwindle. The promise to Abraham (Gen. 15:5) is marching forward, and no Pharaoh can stop it.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to his people, "Behold, the people of Israel are too many and too mighty for us."
verseByVerse.commentary: Pharaoh fears the very blessing of God. The fruitfulness that fulfills the Abrahamic promise looks, to the eye of unbelief, like a threat to be crushed. The world often perceives the growth of God's people as danger rather than gift.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore they set taskmasters over them to afflict them with heavy burdens. They built for Pharaoh store cities, Pithom and Raamses.
verseByVerse.commentary: The strategy of oppression begins. Yet, as Begg notes, the kingdoms of this world cannot enslave the purposes of God; the bricks of Pharaoh's store cities will outlast neither him nor his dynasty, but the people he afflicts will inherit a promise.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-14 — The Pharaoh Who Did Not Know Joseph
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A new dynasty forgets the deliverer Joseph and fears the people he saved. Egypt enslaves Israel with rigorous bondage, but the harder they press, the more Israel multiplies.
verseByVerse.theology: Human kingdoms set themselves against God's people, but their schemes recoil; the more the church is pressed, the more it spreads (cf. Acts 8).
verseByVerse.examples: Tertullian's line holds: the blood of the martyrs is seed. Pressure has never been able to extinguish the people of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who did not know Joseph.
verseByVerse.commentary: The hinge of the chapter. To "not know Joseph" is to forget grace, to treat the savior of the nation as a forgotten footnote. The world's amnesia toward God's mercies always turns toward hostility against God's people.

verseByVerse.quote: But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and the more they spread abroad. And the Egyptians were in dread of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: A divine irony. Pharaoh's strategy backfires under the hidden hand of God. The slavemaster's whip becomes, in God's providence, the very instrument of Israel's growth. The empire dreads what it cannot control.

verseByVerse.quote: and made their lives bitter with hard service, in mortar and brick, and in all kinds of work in the field. In all their work they ruthlessly made them work as slaves.
verseByVerse.commentary: The bitterness of bondage is real and unsparing. God does not minimize his people's suffering; he sees it, names it, and will answer it. The God of Exodus is no stranger to the groan of the oppressed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15-22 — The Fear of God Versus the Fear of Pharaoh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pharaoh commands the midwives to kill the Hebrew boys at birth. They refuse, fearing God, and God deals well with them and gives them families of their own.
verseByVerse.theology: The fear of God is the beginning of courage. Where conscience bound to God collides with the commands of men, we must obey God rather than men (Acts 5:29).
verseByVerse.examples: Two named women, Shiphrah and Puah, are remembered forever in Scripture while the mighty Pharaoh is left nameless. God exalts the humble who fear him.

verseByVerse.quote: But the midwives feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them, but let the male children live.
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is the first act of civil disobedience in the Bible, and God honors it. Sinclair Ferguson notes that the fear of God liberates from the fear of man. These women feared the King of heaven more than the king of Egypt, and that holy fear made them brave.

verseByVerse.quote: So God dealt well with the midwives. And the people multiplied and grew very strong.
verseByVerse.commentary: God honors those who fear him. The midwives risked everything, and God blessed them with households of their own (v. 21). Reverence for God is never finally unrewarded; he is no man's debtor.

verseByVerse.quote: And because the midwives feared God, he gave them families.
verseByVerse.commentary: The reward fits the deed: those who preserved the families of Israel are given families of their own. God's providence quietly vindicates the faithful, weaving their obedience into his larger purpose of multiplying his people.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Pharaoh commanded all his people, "Every son that is born to the Hebrews you shall cast into the Nile, but you shall let every daughter live."
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter ends in darkness: a river meant to be a grave. Yet the very Nile Pharaoh weaponizes will soon carry a basket bearing the deliverer. God turns the instrument of death into the cradle of salvation — a pattern that finds its end at the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, each with his household... And Joseph died, and all his brothers and all that generation.
verseByVerse.commentary: The book of Exodus opens with a backward glance and a forward shadow. The names listed are the covenant family — twelve sons, seventy persons — the seed of Abraham planted in the soil of Egypt. The word names is the Hebrew title for this entire book (Shemot). God knows every name. The seventy who entered Egypt as welcome guests would become a nation of slaves. But note: the text does not begin with the oppression. It begins with the covenant family in place. God is building toward something. The death of Joseph and his entire generation is recorded simply, without drama — because the drama is coming.

verseByVerse.quote: Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, lest they multiply, and, if war breaks out, they join our enemies and fight against us and escape from the land.
verseByVerse.commentary: Pharaoh's fear is the engine of the entire narrative that follows. He does not fear Israel's God; he fears Israel's numbers. His logic is impeccable by human calculation: a large foreign population inside your borders is a security threat. Deal shrewdly — the same Hebrew word used of the serpent in Genesis 3. Pharaoh's wisdom is serpent-wisdom: cunning, self-protective, ultimately self-defeating. Every attempt he makes to reduce Israel will increase them. He is fighting the blessing of Genesis 1:28.

verseByVerse.quote: So they ruthlessly made the people of Israel work as slaves and made their lives bitter with hard service, in mortar and brick, and in all kinds of work in the field.
verseByVerse.commentary: The word ruthlessly (perech) means crushing harshness — the kind of labor that breaks the body and the spirit. Israel builds Pharaoh's store cities with their own hands and their own backs. The irony will only be recognized in retrospect: the same nation enslaved to build Egyptian monuments will build, at God's command, the tabernacle — a dwelling place for the living God. The slave camp becomes the training ground for a nation of craftsmen. But first they must learn, in the depths of affliction, to cry out to the God who hears.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives, one of whom was named Shiphrah and the other Puah, When you serve as midwife to the Hebrew women and see them on the birthstool, if it is a son, you shall kill him, but if it is a daughter, she shall live.
verseByVerse.commentary: Pharaoh's second strategy is genocide disguised as a routine medical order. He gives the command to Shiphrah and Puah — and here the narrator does something extraordinary: he names the midwives. Pharaoh, the great king with his vast bureaucracy and armies, goes unnamed in this story. The midwives who defy him are named forever. God's economy of honor is the inverse of the world's. These two women, at the risk of their own lives, stand between Pharaoh's decree and the children of the promise.

verseByVerse.quote: So the king of Egypt called the midwives and said to them, Why have you done this, and let the male children live? The midwives said to Pharaoh, Because the Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before the midwife comes to them.
verseByVerse.commentary: Whether the midwives' answer is literally true or a cover story, the text is unambiguous about their motivation: they feared God (v.17). Their fear of God was greater than their fear of Pharaoh. This is the first act of civil disobedience in Israel's story, and it is performed by women who have no political power, no army, and no protection except the fear of the LORD. God rewards their faithfulness by building them households — the very thing Pharaoh was trying to prevent for all of Israel. What Pharaoh destroys, God builds.

1.theology:
The faithfulness of God to his promises. The growth of Israel is the keeping of the Abrahamic covenant (Gen. 12, 15). No empire can annul what God has sworn. The whole book rests on this bedrock: God remembers.

The fear of God. Shiphrah and Puah embody the truth that reverence for God is the root of moral courage. To fear God is to be set free from the tyranny of fear of man.

Suffering and providence. God's people are not promised ease but presence. Affliction is real, yet it is woven into a providence that advances, not defeats, God's purposes.
1.examples:
Then: A favored immigrant people became despised slaves under a regime that feared their numbers and sought their extinction — the first genocide recorded in Scripture, met by the quiet defiance of God-fearing women.

Now: Christians under pressure should not be surprised. The church grows where it is persecuted. And we are called, like the midwives, to a higher allegiance: to fear God so deeply that the threats of the powerful lose their grip on us.

2.title: Drawn Out of the Water
2.text: <sup>2</sup>The woman conceived and bore a son, and when she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months. <sup>10</sup>When the child grew older, she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, "Because," she said, "I drew him out of the water." <sup>23</sup>...and the people of Israel groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help. Their cry for rescue from slavery came up to God. <sup>24</sup>And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob. <sup>25</sup>God saw the people of Israel—and God knew.
2.overview:
Against Pharaoh's death-decree, God begins his rescue not with armies but with a baby in a basket. A Levite woman hides her son, then entrusts him to the very river meant to drown him, in a little ark of bulrushes daubed with pitch — the same word used of Noah's ark. The deliverer is saved by water that should have killed him, and is drawn from it by the daughter of the very tyrant who ordered his death. Providence has a sense of irony and a sovereign hand.

Moses grows up in two worlds — nursed by his Hebrew mother, raised in Pharaoh's palace. As Hebrews 11 tells us, he will one day choose to be mistreated with the people of God rather than enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin. But first comes his failed attempt to deliver by his own hand: he kills an Egyptian, is exposed, and flees to Midian. The man who tries to save Israel in his own strength must spend forty years in the wilderness learning that salvation belongs to the LORD.

The chapter closes with four of the most tender verbs in Scripture: God heard, God remembered, God saw, God knew. The silence of heaven is about to break.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-10 — The Basket on the Nile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A Levite couple hides their son, then sets him afloat in a waterproofed basket. Pharaoh's own daughter finds him, and his mother is hired to nurse him. He is named Moses, drawn out of the water.
verseByVerse.theology: God's saving purposes ride on the smallest providences — a basket, a sister's watchfulness, a princess's pity. He chooses the weak to shame the strong.
verseByVerse.examples: The deliverer is rescued through water under sentence of death — an early shadow of the greater Deliverer who would pass through death and water to save his people.

verseByVerse.quote: The woman conceived and bore a son, and when she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months.
verseByVerse.commentary: Faith dares. Hebrews 11:23 says his parents hid him "because they saw that the child was beautiful, and they were not afraid of the king's edict." A mother's faith stands against an emperor's decree.

verseByVerse.quote: When she could hide him no longer, she took for him a basket made of bulrushes and daubed it with bitumen and pitch. She put the child in it and placed it among the reeds by the river bank.
verseByVerse.commentary: The word for "basket" is the same Hebrew word as Noah's "ark." Both are vessels of salvation through judgment-waters. God preserves his chosen through the very flood meant to destroy them.

verseByVerse.quote: Now the daughter of Pharaoh came down to bathe at the river, while her young women walked beside the river bank. She saw the basket among the reeds and sent her servant woman, and she took it.
verseByVerse.commentary: Providence weaves its web. Of all places, Pharaoh's own daughter comes to the very spot where the deliverer floats. The God who governs empires governs also the steps of a princess to a riverbank, bending the tyrant's household toward the rescue of his people.

verseByVerse.quote: When she opened it, she saw the child, and behold, the baby was crying. She took pity on him and said, "This is one of the Hebrews' children."
verseByVerse.commentary: Compassion stirs in the heart of an Egyptian for a condemned Hebrew child. God can plant mercy in the most unlikely heart to accomplish his saving purpose. The tears of a baby move the daughter of his executioner.

verseByVerse.quote: ...She named him Moses, "Because," she said, "I drew him out of the water."
verseByVerse.commentary: The name means "drawn out" — and Moses will spend his life drawing a people out: out of water, out of Egypt, out of bondage. The savior bears the name of the salvation he brings.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 11-22 — The Failed Deliverer in Exile
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses kills an Egyptian who is beating a Hebrew, is rejected by his own people, and flees to Midian, where he marries and tends sheep — a prince become a shepherd in the desert.
verseByVerse.theology: Self-made deliverance fails. Moses must be emptied of Egypt's strength before he can be filled with God's. Forty years in the wilderness are not wasted — they are God's seminary.
verseByVerse.examples: Like Moses rejected by his brothers, Christ "came to his own, and his own people did not receive him" (John 1:11). Stephen draws this parallel directly in Acts 7.

verseByVerse.quote: He looked this way and that, and seeing no one, he struck down the Egyptian and hid him in the sand.
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses tries to be a savior on his own terms, in his own timing, by his own violence. The man who looks "this way and that" forgets the One who sees all. Self-reliance is the death of true deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: One day, when Moses had grown up, he went out to his people and looked on their burdens, and he saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his people.
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses identifies with his suffering people — Hebrews 11:24-26 says he chose to be mistreated with the people of God rather than enjoy the fleeting pleasures of sin and the treasures of Egypt. Yet his zeal, untempered by God's timing, runs ahead into violence.

verseByVerse.quote: He answered, "Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you mean to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?" Then Moses was afraid, and thought, "Surely the thing is known."
verseByVerse.commentary: Rejected by his own, the would-be deliverer must flee. Stephen draws the parallel to Christ (Acts 7:25-35): the people did not understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand. Moses, like Christ, is first refused before he delivers.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 23-25 — God Heard, Remembered, Saw, Knew
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The old Pharaoh dies, but the slavery continues. Israel groans, and their cry rises to God, who hears, remembers his covenant, sees them, and knows.
verseByVerse.theology: God's remembering is never mere recollection; it is covenant faithfulness moving into action. To say "God knew" is to say he engaged himself personally with his suffering people.
verseByVerse.examples: When the church cries out in affliction, heaven is not silent. The God of Exodus still hears the groaning of his people and moves to act on covenant love.

verseByVerse.quote: And God heard their groaning, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, with Isaac, and with Jacob.
verseByVerse.commentary: The turning point of the book. As Derek Kidner observes, God's "remembering" is not the waking of a forgetful deity but the activating of a sworn promise. The covenant made centuries earlier now becomes the engine of redemption.

verseByVerse.quote: God saw the people of Israel—and God knew.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Hebrew breaks off almost mid-thought: "and God knew." Knew what? Everything — their pain, their need, his own purpose. It is the pregnant pause before the storm of salvation. The next chapter is the burning bush.

verseByVerse.quote: Now a man from the house of Levi went and took as his wife a Levite woman. The woman conceived and bore a son, and when she saw that he was a fine child, she hid him three months.
verseByVerse.commentary: The birth of Moses is narrated with remarkable understatement: no angelic announcement, no dramatic sign. A Levite man, a Levite woman, a child born. The mother sees that he is fine (tov — the same word used of creation in Genesis 1: God saw that it was good). She hides him. The act of hiding is an act of faith against the decree of an empire. Hebrews 11 will call it faith: By faith Moses, when he was born, was hidden for three months by his parents. The ark of bulrushes echoes Noah's ark: another vessel prepared by faith to carry the covenant people through the waters of judgment.

verseByVerse.quote: Then his sister said to Pharaoh's daughter, Shall I go and call you a nurse from the Hebrew women to nurse the child for you? And Pharaoh's daughter said to her, Go. So the girl went and called the child's mother.
verseByVerse.commentary: The providence of God in this passage is almost playful. Moses' sister watches from a distance, then steps forward at exactly the right moment. The result is miraculous: the child's own mother is paid by Pharaoh's household to nurse and raise the son Pharaoh tried to kill. The empire funds the rescue of its own deliverer. Pharaoh's daughter names him Moses — drawn out — without knowing she has named the one who will draw an entire nation out of Egypt. God arranges his purposes through the instincts of a protective sister, the compassion of an Egyptian princess, and the milk of a Hebrew mother.

verseByVerse.quote: When he went out the next day, behold, two Hebrews were quarreling. And he said to the man in the wrong, Why do you strike your fellow Hebrew? He answered, Who made you a prince and a judge over us? Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses' first attempt at leadership ends in rejection and exile. He saw an injustice, he acted, and the man he was trying to defend turns on him: who made you a prince and a judge? The question is premature — God will make him exactly that — but the timing is wrong. Stephen in Acts 7 comments that Moses supposed his brothers would understand that God was giving them salvation by his hand, but they did not understand. The forty years in Midian that follow are not a detour from Moses' calling; they are the school in which God prepares him for it.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses fled from Pharaoh and stayed in the land of Midian. And he sat down by a well... Now the priest of Midian had seven daughters, and they came and drew water and filled the troughs to water their father's flock.
verseByVerse.commentary: The pattern of Moses at the well echoes Jacob and Isaac's servant — the well is where covenant history happens. He defends the daughters of Reuel (Jethro) from other shepherds, an act of the same impulse that led him to defend the Hebrew slave. He is given a home, a wife, a son. He names his son Gershom — I have been a sojourner in a foreign land. The name is grief and honesty: he knows he does not belong in Midian any more than he belonged in Egypt's court. He is a man between worlds, waiting. In verse 23, the long parenthesis of his Midian years is closed by a single verse: the people of Israel groaned because of their slavery and cried out for help. Their cry came up to God. And God heard.

2.theology:
Providence. Every detail — a basket, a sister, a princess's compassion — is governed by an unseen hand bending Pharaoh's own household toward Israel's rescue.

The weakness of the flesh. Moses' premature, violent attempt at deliverance must fail so that God's deliverance may stand. Salvation is the LORD's, not the deliverer's.

Covenant remembrance. God hears, remembers, sees, and knows. His saving acts flow from his covenant faithfulness, not from Israel's worthiness.
2.examples:
Then: Under a death decree, God preserved a deliverer through the very waters of judgment, raised him in the enemy's house, then drove him into forty years of obscurity to prepare him.

Now: God still uses long, hidden seasons to empty us of self-confidence and fit us for his service. And he still hears the cry of his afflicted people — our groaning is never lost in the silence.

3.title: I AM WHO I AM
3.text: <sup>2</sup>And the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush was burning, yet it was not consumed. <sup>5</sup>Then he said, "Do not come near; take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground." <sup>7</sup>Then the LORD said, "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry... <sup>8</sup>and I have come down to deliver them." <sup>14</sup>God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM." And he said, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'I AM has sent me to you.'"
3.overview:
Here is one of the holiest moments in all of Scripture. An eighty-year-old shepherd, long since written off, turns aside to see a bush that burns but is not consumed — and meets the living God. The fire that does not consume is a parable of God himself: blazing in holiness, yet not destroying; full of glory, yet stooping to speak with a fugitive on the back side of the desert.

God reveals his compassion before he reveals his name: "I have surely seen... I have heard... I have come down to deliver." The transcendent God of the bush is also the God who bends to the cries of slaves. Then comes the name above all names: "I AM WHO I AM" — the self-existent, eternal, unchanging God who depends on nothing and on whom all things depend. Sproul called this the most important text on the being of God in the Old Testament. The God of the burning bush is the God who simply IS.

When Jesus later says, "Before Abraham was, I am" (John 8:58), he claims this very name. The voice from the bush and the voice in Galilee are one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses, tending Jethro's flock, sees the burning bush and turns aside. God calls his name, commands him to remove his sandals, and identifies himself as the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses hides his face.
verseByVerse.theology: God is holy, and his presence makes ordinary ground holy. The right response to the manifest presence of God is reverent fear, not casual familiarity.
verseByVerse.examples: The burning-but-unconsumed bush pictures God dwelling with sinful people without destroying them — a mystery answered only at the cross, where holiness and mercy meet.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire out of the midst of a bush. He looked, and behold, the bush was burning, yet it was not consumed.
verseByVerse.commentary: Fire in Scripture signals God's holy presence. A lowly desert bush — not a cedar of Lebanon — is chosen to bear the flame, just as God chooses the weak and lowly. Calvin saw here a picture of the church: afflicted, aflame, yet never consumed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said, "Do not come near; take your sandals off your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground."
verseByVerse.commentary: Holiness demands distance and reverence. Before Moses can be sent, he must be humbled. The same God who says "come" first says "do not come near" — access to the holy is always on God's terms, never our own.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "I am the God of your father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." And Moses hid his face, for he was afraid to look at God.
verseByVerse.commentary: God roots his self-revelation in covenant history. Jesus cites this very verse to prove the resurrection (Matt. 22:32): God is not the God of the dead but of the living. The patriarchs live still, for the covenant God does not let his people perish.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-12 — I Have Come Down to Deliver
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God declares that he has seen, heard, and known Israel's suffering, and has come down to deliver them into a good land. He commissions Moses, who protests, "Who am I?" God answers, "I will be with you."
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption is initiated by God's compassion, not human merit. The one assurance for the called servant is not his own adequacy but God's presence.
verseByVerse.examples: "I have come down to deliver" is the gospel pattern fulfilled in the incarnation: the God who comes down to rescue his people from a bondage deeper than Egypt.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said, "I have surely seen the affliction of my people who are in Egypt and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters. I know their sufferings."
verseByVerse.commentary: Three verbs of divine tenderness: seen, heard, know. Keller observes that God does not save his people from a distance; he enters into their suffering. The compassion of the bush anticipates the compassion of the manger.

verseByVerse.quote: and I have come down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians and to bring them up out of that land to a good and broad land...
verseByVerse.commentary: "I have come down." This is the great movement of redemption — God descending to rescue. It will reach its climax when the Word is made flesh and dwells among us (John 1:14).

verseByVerse.quote: Come, I will send you to Pharaoh that you may bring my people, the people of Israel, out of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary: The God who comes down to deliver chooses to deliver through a sent man. Divine sovereignty does not bypass human instruments; it commissions them. The great I AM sends a shepherd, and the shepherd's adequacy lies wholly in the One who sends.

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "But I will be with you, and this shall be the sign for you, that I have sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you shall serve God on this mountain."
verseByVerse.commentary: The one sufficient credential is God's presence: "I will be with you." Sinclair Ferguson notes that this promise — Immanuel in seed — is the bedrock of every calling. The servant's confidence rests not in himself but in the God who goes with him.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses asks for God's name. God reveals himself as "I AM WHO I AM," the LORD (YHWH), the God of the fathers, his name forever. He promises Moses success and that Israel will plunder Egypt.
verseByVerse.theology: God's name reveals his self-existence, eternality, and unchanging faithfulness. He is the ground of all being, dependent on nothing, the same yesterday, today, and forever.
verseByVerse.examples: Jesus' "I am" sayings in John deliberately echo this name; to claim it is to claim deity. The God of the bush is the God of Bethlehem.

verseByVerse.quote: God said to Moses, "I AM WHO I AM." And he said, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'I AM has sent me to you.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The most profound self-disclosure in the Old Testament. God is pure being, underived, eternal, self-sufficient. Sproul taught that here God declares his aseity — he is from himself, in need of nothing. And this infinite I AM stoops to send a shepherd to slaves.

verseByVerse.quote: God also said to Moses, "Say this to the people of Israel: 'The LORD, the God of your fathers... has sent me to you.' This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations."
verseByVerse.commentary: The name YHWH, built on the verb "to be," is God's covenant name forever. Calvin observed that here God gives his people not merely information but a name to call upon — a personal God who binds himself to be remembered and trusted across all generations.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Moses was keeping the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian, and he led his flock to the west side of the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The greatest commission in human history begins with a man doing ordinary work. Moses has been a shepherd in Midian for forty years. There is nothing extraordinary about the day, or the route, or the mountain — except that God is there. The mountain of God is Horeb/Sinai, where the law will later be given. Moses arrives not because he is seeking a vision but because he is doing his job. God finds his servants in the ordinary. The burning bush that is not consumed is not first a symbol to be decoded but a sight to be seen — and Moses says, I will turn aside to see this great sight. His curiosity saves him. Those who will not turn aside miss the burning bush entirely.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said, I will turn aside to see this great sight, why the bush is not burned. When the LORD saw that he turned aside to see, God called to him out of the bush.
verseByVerse.commentary: The conditional form is worth noting: when the LORD saw that he turned aside. God waited to see if Moses would respond. The divine call comes to the man who is paying attention, who interrupts his routine to investigate something that should not be possible. Sproul notes that this is the pattern of divine encounter throughout Scripture: God speaks to those who stop and listen. The name called twice — Moses, Moses — is the form used when God summons a person for something urgent and holy. Abraham heard it; Israel will hear it at Sinai.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, behold, the cry of the people of Israel has come to me, and I have also seen the oppression with which the Egyptians oppress them. Come, I will send you to Pharaoh that you may bring my people, the children of Israel, out of Egypt. But Moses said to God, Who am I that I should go to Pharaoh?
verseByVerse.commentary: God's commission contains the entire theology of redemption in miniature: I have seen, I have heard, I have come down, I will send you. The initiative is entirely God's. Moses' objection — Who am I? — is not false humility but honest self-assessment. The man who once thought he could lead Israel by his own initiative now knows he cannot. God's answer is not a flattering assessment of Moses' qualifications but a promise: I will be with you. The sign confirming the mission will only come after the mission is completed — you shall worship God on this mountain. God asks Moses to act on the promise before the sign is given. This is what faith looks like.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses said to God, If I come to the people of Israel and say to them, The God of your fathers has sent me to you, and they ask me, What is his name? what shall I say to them? God said to Moses, I AM WHO I AM.
verseByVerse.commentary: The divine name revealed at the burning bush is the most theologically dense moment in the Old Testament. I AM WHO I AM — YHWH — is the name that cannot be reduced to a category, cannot be subordinated to a system, cannot be manipulated by formula. He simply is. All being derives from him; he derives his being from nothing. The rabbis counted it the most holy name; the Jews eventually would not pronounce it. Jesus will pick up the same formulation: before Abraham was, I am. The one standing in the burning bush and the one who says I am the bread of life, the light of the world, the resurrection and the life — are the same I AM.

verseByVerse.quote: Go and gather the elders of Israel together and say to them, The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob, has appeared to me... And I know that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless compelled by a mighty hand.
verseByVerse.commentary: God gives Moses the full briefing: what to say to the elders, what to say to Pharaoh, what will happen (Pharaoh will refuse), how God will respond (wonders and judgment), and what the final result will be (Israel will go out with great plunder). The plundering of Egypt echoes the blessing of Abraham: your offspring shall come out with great possessions (Gen. 15:14). Everything has been planned before Moses asks a single question. The mission will unfold exactly as God said. The servant's role is not to figure out the plan but to trust it.

3.theology:
The holiness of God. The fire, the holy ground, the hidden face — all proclaim that God is set apart, unapproachable except on his own terms.

The aseity and eternity of God. "I AM WHO I AM" reveals a God who simply is — self-existent, unchanging, the source of all being.

The compassion of God. The transcendent I AM is also the God who has seen, heard, and come down. Holiness and mercy meet in the bush as they will meet at the cross.
3.examples:
Then: A discarded fugitive met the eternal God in a desert and was commissioned to confront an empire — armed with nothing but a name and a promise: "I will be with you."

Now: The same I AM meets us in Christ. When we feel inadequate to our calling — "Who am I?" — the answer is not our resume but his presence. The God who is enough has promised to be with us.

4.title: The Sufficiency of God in Our Weakness
4.text: <sup>10</sup>But Moses said to the LORD, "Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent... but I am slow of speech and of tongue." <sup>11</sup>Then the LORD said to him, "Who has made man's mouth? ... Is it not I, the LORD? <sup>12</sup>Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak." <sup>22</sup>Then you shall say to Pharaoh, "Thus says the LORD, Israel is my firstborn son... <sup>23</sup>let my son go that he may serve me."
4.overview:
Moses meets the call of God with a string of excuses: they won't believe me; I'm not eloquent; please send someone else. To each objection God answers not by flattering Moses but by revealing more of himself — his power over signs, his lordship over the human mouth, his promise to be present. The lesson is bracing: God's calling rests on God's sufficiency, not ours. As Begg often says, God does not call the equipped; he equips the called.

God gives Moses three signs — the staff that becomes a serpent, the leprous hand, the water turned to blood — visible proofs that the I AM has sent him. When Moses still pleads inadequacy, God's anger is kindled, yet even his displeasure bends toward grace: he gives Aaron as a mouthpiece. God will accomplish his purpose, with or without our willing cooperation, but he delights to use surrendered servants.

The chapter introduces a staggering phrase: "Israel is my firstborn son." The exodus is not merely a slave rebellion; it is a Father reclaiming his child. And the demand — "let my son go that he may serve me" — sets the true purpose of redemption: not merely freedom from, but freedom for the worship of God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-9 — Three Signs for a Doubting Servant
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God answers Moses' fear that Israel will not believe him by giving three signs: the staff-to-serpent, the leprous-then-healed hand, and water-to-blood. These authenticate Moses as God's sent one.
verseByVerse.theology: God condescends to our weakness with confirming signs, but the signs point beyond themselves to his power and word.
verseByVerse.examples: The God who controls serpents, disease, and the Nile will soon turn all three against Egypt. The signs are previews of the plagues.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to him, "What is that in your hand?" He said, "A staff."
verseByVerse.commentary: God begins with what Moses already holds. The ordinary shepherd's staff, surrendered to God, becomes the rod of God that parts seas and strikes rocks. God takes the little we have and makes it mighty in his hand.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said, "Throw it on the ground." So he threw it on the ground, and it became a serpent, and Moses ran from it.
verseByVerse.commentary: The familiar staff becomes a serpent, and Moses flees from what he held moments before. God shows that the ordinary, surrendered to him, can become both fearsome and mighty. What we grip in our own hands becomes new in his.

verseByVerse.quote: "...that they may believe that the LORD, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has appeared to you."
verseByVerse.commentary: The signs serve faith — that the people may believe the covenant God has truly sent Moses. God graciously accommodates human weakness with confirming wonders, yet the signs point beyond themselves to his word and his name.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses pleads that he is not eloquent. God reminds him that he made the mouth and will be with it. When Moses still refuses, God's anger is kindled, yet he graciously provides Aaron to speak.
verseByVerse.theology: Our inadequacies are no surprise to the God who created us; he calls us not because of our gifts but to display his power. To plead inability is, in truth, to question the Creator.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul's testimony echoes here: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness" (2 Cor. 12:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to him, "Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD?"
verseByVerse.commentary: A staggering claim of sovereignty over every human faculty and limitation. Sproul noted that God here takes responsibility even for human disability — a hard truth that drives us to trust his wisdom. The Maker of the mouth can certainly fill it.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak.
verseByVerse.commentary: The promise to Moses is the promise to every herald of God's word: "I will be with your mouth." Jesus repeats it to his disciples (Luke 12:12). We are not left to our own eloquence; the Spirit teaches us what to say.

verseByVerse.quote: But he said, "Oh, my Lord, please send someone else."
verseByVerse.commentary: The naked heart of the excuse-maker. Behind all the reasons lies an unwilling heart. God's anger is kindled — yet his grace still provides Aaron. He overrules our reluctance without excusing it.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the anger of the LORD was kindled against Moses and he said, "Is there not Aaron, your brother, the Levite? I know that he can speak well..."
verseByVerse.commentary: God's anger is kindled at Moses' unwilling heart, yet even his displeasure bends toward provision: he gives Aaron as a mouthpiece. God overrules our reluctance without excusing it, accomplishing his purpose through faltering servants.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18-31 — Return to Egypt and the Firstborn Son
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses returns to Egypt. God forewarns that he will harden Pharaoh's heart and declares Israel his firstborn son, threatening Egypt's firstborn. After a strange and sobering episode, the people believe and worship.
verseByVerse.theology: God's sovereignty extends even over Pharaoh's hardening, and his fatherly love names Israel his firstborn. Redemption is a Father claiming his son for worship.
verseByVerse.examples: "Israel is my firstborn son" anticipates the true firstborn, Jesus Christ, the Son who is given so that we might be adopted as sons.

verseByVerse.quote: Then you shall say to Pharaoh, 'Thus says the LORD, Israel is my firstborn son,
verseByVerse.commentary: The exodus is reframed as a family rescue. Israel is no mere ethnic group but God's beloved son. Carson notes that adoption-language threads from here to the New Testament, where in Christ we too are made sons and heirs.

verseByVerse.quote: And the people believed; and when they heard that the LORD had visited the people of Israel and that he had seen their affliction, they bowed their heads and worshiped.
verseByVerse.commentary: The people believe and worship — God has seen their affliction. The right response to the news that God has come down to deliver is to bow and adore. So the gospel, received, brings the bowed head and the worshiping heart.

verseByVerse.quote: and I say to you, "Let my son go that he may serve me." If you refuse to let him go, behold, I will kill your firstborn son.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The purpose of deliverance is service — worship. And the warning of the final plague is sounded already. The freedom God gives is never freedom for ourselves; it is freedom to serve the God who redeemed us.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses answered, But behold, they will not believe me or listen to my voice, for they will say, The LORD did not appear to you.
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses' second objection is practical: what if they don't believe me? God's answer is three signs — the staff becoming a serpent, the leprous hand, the water turning to blood. These are not tricks; they are previews of the plagues to come. The staff that becomes a serpent foreshadows Pharaoh, himself serpentine, whose magicians can duplicate the sign but whose serpent-staff is swallowed by Aaron's (7:12). God is answering Moses' doubts about Israel's faith by giving him the very signs that will eventually break Pharaoh. The tools for both tasks are given at once.

verseByVerse.quote: Again, the LORD said to him, Put your hand inside your cloak. And he put his hand inside his cloak, and when he took it out, behold, his hand was leprous like snow.
verseByVerse.commentary: The leprous hand — instantly diseased, instantly restored — is the LORD demonstrating that he is Lord over affliction and healing both. He who can strike with disease can remove it; he who brings darkness can restore light. This will be the repeated logic of the plagues: God controls what Egypt's gods claimed to control. The sign is given to Moses personally before it is given to anyone else. He must see God's power before he can display it. The servant must first believe the message before he can credibly deliver it.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall speak to him and put the words in his mouth, and I will be with your mouth and with his mouth and will teach you both what to do. He shall speak for you to the people, and he himself shall be your mouth, and you shall be as God to him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Aaron's appointment as Moses' spokesman solves Moses' final objection (I am not eloquent) while establishing the pattern of the prophetic office: the prophet is the mouth of God to the people, speaking words given to him from above. Moses will be as God to Aaron; Aaron will be to the people what Moses is to Aaron. The chain of mediation is already being established, pointing toward the ultimate Mediator who is both God and man — who needs no chain because he speaks from himself with full authority: I tell you the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: At a lodging place on the way the LORD met him and sought to put him to death. Then Zipporah took a flint and cut off her son's foreskin and touched Moses' feet with it and said, Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me.
verseByVerse.commentary: This is one of the most enigmatic and unsettling passages in Exodus. Moses — just commissioned as God's deliverer — nearly dies because his son has not been circumcised. The covenant sign given to Abraham has been neglected. Zipporah acts decisively, performing the circumcision herself, and the crisis passes. Kidner observes that the incident is a warning: even the deliverer is not exempt from the covenant's demands. The one sent to confront Pharaoh about Israel's covenant standing must himself be in covenant standing. No one is above the sign of the blood.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Aaron, Go into the wilderness to meet Moses. So he went and met him at the mountain of God and kissed him. And Moses told Aaron all the words of the LORD with which he had sent him to speak, and all the signs that he had commanded him to do.
verseByVerse.commentary: The two brothers meet at the mountain of God — the same mountain where the burning bush appeared, the same mountain where the law will be given. Aaron's greeting is a kiss of reunion after years apart. Moses debriefs his brother: all the words, all the signs. Then together they go to the elders. The people believe. They bow their heads and worship. The first act of the delivered people is worship — and it happens before a single plague has fallen, before a single chain has been broken. They believe the word before they see the deed. This is faith.

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to the LORD, Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent, either in the past or since you have spoken to your servant, but I am slow of speech and of tongue.
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses' objection — I am not eloquent — is the most honest thing he says in this chapter. He is not making excuses; he is describing himself accurately. And God's response is stunning: Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD? The Creator of the capacity is not limited by its deficiencies. God does not need eloquent servants; he needs obedient ones. He will fill the mouth he made. The stammer of Moses will become the thunder of Sinai.

4.theology:
The sufficiency of God in human weakness. God's call rests on his power, not the servant's gifts. "Who made man's mouth?" silences every excuse.

Divine sovereignty. God claims authority over speech, disability, Pharaoh's heart, and the outcome of history. Nothing lies outside his rule.

Redemption unto worship. "Let my son go that he may serve me." Salvation's goal is not mere liberation but the worship of God.
4.examples:
Then: A reluctant shepherd, full of excuses, was sent to confront a superpower, assured only that the God who made his mouth would go with him.

Now: When God calls us beyond our competence, the question is never "Am I able?" but "Is God able?" Our weakness is the stage for his strength. And we are redeemed not for ourselves but to serve and worship our Redeemer.

5.title: When Obedience Makes Things Worse
5.text: <sup>1</sup>Afterward Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.'" <sup>2</sup>But Pharaoh said, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go." <sup>22</sup>Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, "O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me?"
5.overview:
The first confrontation goes badly. Moses and Aaron deliver God's word — "Let my people go" — and Pharaoh responds with the defiant question that defines all human rebellion: "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice?" Pharaoh, worshiped as a god in Egypt, will not bow to the God of slaves. So he doubles the burden: the Israelites must now gather their own straw while meeting the same quota of bricks.

The result is that obedience to God makes things, for the moment, far worse. The Israelite foremen turn on Moses; Moses turns on God: "Why did you ever send me?" This is the dark valley every believer eventually walks — when doing the right thing brings not relief but trouble, and faith is stretched to its breaking point. Ferguson reminds us that God's deliverances often deepen before they dawn; the darkest hour is just before the outstretched arm.

The chapter teaches us that God's timetable is not ours, and that the lowest point of our circumstances may be precisely the threshold of his greatest work.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses and Aaron demand release for worship. Pharaoh defiantly denies knowing the LORD and increases Israel's labor, accusing them of laziness.
verseByVerse.theology: Pharaoh's question, "Who is the LORD?", is the essence of unbelief. The whole book of Exodus will be God's answer — Egypt will know him by his mighty acts.
verseByVerse.examples: Hard-hearted rulers and cultures still ask Pharaoh's question. The answer comes not in argument alone but in God's vindication of his own name.

verseByVerse.quote: Afterward Moses and Aaron went and said to Pharaoh, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Let my people go, that they may hold a feast to me in the wilderness.'"
verseByVerse.commentary: The demand is for worship, not merely freedom. The aim of redemption from the start is a feast to the LORD. God frees slaves so they may become worshipers.

verseByVerse.quote: Then they said, "The God of the Hebrews has met with us. Please let us go a three days' journey into the wilderness that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God, lest he fall upon us with pestilence or with the sword."
verseByVerse.commentary: The request centers on worship — sacrifice to the LORD. From the outset, the goal of deliverance is not mere liberty but worship. God frees his people that they may serve and adore him.

verseByVerse.quote: But Pharaoh said, "Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice and let Israel go? I do not know the LORD, and moreover, I will not let Israel go."
verseByVerse.commentary: The defining sentence of human pride. Pharaoh will say it now in arrogance; by the end he will know the LORD in judgment. As Calvin notes, all rebellion is at root a refusal to acknowledge God's authority over us.

verseByVerse.quote: But the king of Egypt said to them, "Moses and Aaron, why do you take the people away from their work? Get back to your burdens."
verseByVerse.commentary: Pharaoh reduces God's people to their economic usefulness — units of labor, not image-bearers. The tyranny of this world always sees worship as wasted productivity. But man's chief end is to glorify God, not to serve Pharaoh's quotas.

verseByVerse.quote: "You shall no longer give the people straw to make bricks, as in the past; let them go and gather straw for themselves."
verseByVerse.commentary: The cruelty escalates precisely because God's word has been spoken. As Ferguson observes, the first effect of God's deliverance is often increased pressure, as the enemy tightens his grip before the great release.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Pharaoh withholds straw but demands the same quota. The Israelite foremen are beaten and then turn in bitterness against Moses and Aaron for making them odious to Pharaoh.
verseByVerse.theology: When God's people begin to obey, opposition often intensifies. The enemy presses hardest just as deliverance draws near.
verseByVerse.examples: Spiritual progress frequently provokes increased trial. The Christian who begins to follow Christ may find life harder, not easier, at first.

verseByVerse.quote: and they said to them, "The LORD look on you and judge, because you have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh and his servants, and have put a sword in their hand to kill us."
verseByVerse.commentary: The people blame the messengers. How quickly the oppressed turn on their deliverer when deliverance costs. This rejection prefigures Israel's repeated grumbling — and ultimately the rejection of the greater Deliverer.

verseByVerse.quote: For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all."
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses speaks with raw honesty: "you have not delivered your people at all." Faith in the dark may not yet see the deliverance, but it still addresses God. The lament is itself a confession that deliverance is God's to give.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses brings his confusion and disappointment straight to God: Why have you done evil to this people? Why did you send me? God has only made things worse.
verseByVerse.theology: Faith can wrestle honestly with God in the dark. Lament that turns toward God, not away from him, is itself an act of trust.
verseByVerse.examples: The Psalms are full of such honest cries. God invites us to bring our bewilderment to him rather than nursing it in silence.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, "O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Note where Moses turns — "to the LORD." His complaint is also a prayer. Begg observes that the mark of faith is not the absence of confusion but the direction of our complaint: we take it to the throne, not to despair.

verseByVerse.quote: And Pharaoh said, Behold, the people of the land are now many, and you make them rest from their burdens! The same day Pharaoh commanded the taskmasters of the people and their foremen, You shall no longer give the people straw to make bricks, as in the past; let them go and gather straw for themselves.
verseByVerse.commentary: The immediate result of Moses' first demand is not liberation but intensification of oppression. This is the pattern of faith's early obedience: things often get worse before they get better. Pharaoh's logic is the logic of every tyrant: the people have too much time if they can think about God. Remove the straw, keep the quota, break the spirit. His countermove is shrewd and cruel. The people's faith, which had just been expressed in worship (4:31), is now being tested in the furnace of harder labor. Can they believe a God who has let things get worse?

verseByVerse.quote: But the quota of bricks that they made before, you shall impose on them, you shall by no means reduce it, for they are idle. Therefore they cry, Let us go and offer sacrifice to our God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The irony is theological: Pharaoh's diagnosis is that they have too much rest, too much time to think about God. He is accidentally right that worship and slavery cannot coexist — but wrong about which must give way. The taskmasters beat the Israelite foremen who fall short. The foremen come to Pharaoh and are refused. The entire system of oppression lands on the backs of the people themselves through the chain of foremen-overseers-taskmasters. This is how systemic evil works: it makes the oppressed police each other. The foremen then turn on Moses and Aaron with the bitterest words of the book: You have made us stink in the sight of Pharaoh.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses turned to the LORD and said, O Lord, why have you done evil to this people? Why did you ever send me? For since I came to Pharaoh to speak in your name, he has done evil to this people, and you have not delivered your people at all.
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses' complaint to God is raw and honest and entirely understandable. He was sent with a promise; the promise seems to have made things worse. Why have you done evil to this people? This is not the prayer of a man without faith; it is the prayer of a man whose faith is being stretched to its capacity. God does not rebuke Moses for the question. He answers it. The lament psalms that will fill the Psalter are rooted here: the people of God are permitted — even invited — to bring their bewilderment directly to God. The question is not faithlessness; the question that expects an answer from God is itself a form of trust.

5.theology:
The defiance of unbelief. "Who is the LORD?" exposes the heart of rebellion — a refusal to acknowledge God's right to rule.

The cost of obedience. Following God's word can bring immediate hardship. God's deliverances often deepen the darkness before the dawn.

Honest lament. Moses brings his bewilderment to God himself. Faith may wrestle in the dark, so long as it wrestles with God.
5.examples:
Then: The first obedience to God's command brought heavier chains, not freedom, and the deliverer was blamed by the very people he came to save.

Now: When obedience seems to make life harder and prayers seem to go unanswered, we are exactly where Moses stood. The lowest point is often the threshold of God's mightiest work. Bring your "why" to the LORD.

6.title: I Will Redeem You with an Outstretched Arm
6.text: <sup>6</sup>"Say therefore to the people of Israel, 'I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from slavery to them, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment. <sup>7</sup>I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God... <sup>8</sup>I will bring you into the land... I am the LORD.'"
6.overview:
In answer to Moses' despair, God responds not with a new plan but with a renewed revelation of himself. "I am the LORD" frames the passage like a refrain. God recalls his covenant with the patriarchs and then unfurls a magnificent chain of "I will" promises — the so-called seven "I wills" of redemption: I will bring you out, I will deliver you, I will redeem you, I will take you, I will be your God, I will bring you in, I will give you the land. Salvation is spelled out entirely in the first person of God. Every verb belongs to him.

Here the great word redeem enters in force: "I will redeem you with an outstretched arm." To redeem is to buy back, to free at cost, to claim as one's own. The outstretched arm — a recurring image of God's saving power — will reach its fullest stretch on a Roman cross, where the Redeemer's arms are stretched out to purchase a people at the cost of his blood.

Yet the chapter ends realistically: the people, broken in spirit by their slavery, do not listen. God's promises are not finally validated by the faith of his people but by the faithfulness of God himself.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God reassures Moses, recalling that he revealed himself to the patriarchs as God Almighty but now makes known his covenant name, the LORD, and has remembered his covenant in hearing Israel's groaning.
verseByVerse.theology: God's saving acts are grounded in his prior covenant promises. He acts to keep his sworn word, and the unveiling of his name marks a new stage of revelation.
verseByVerse.examples: Redemption is rooted in covenant. God binds himself to a people and then moves heaven and earth to keep faith with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, I have heard the groaning of the people of Israel whom the Egyptians hold as slaves, and I have remembered my covenant.
verseByVerse.commentary: Again that great word: God "remembered." His remembering is covenant in motion. The groaning that rose in chapter 2 has not been forgotten; it is the trigger of the outstretched arm.

verseByVerse.quote: God spoke to Moses and said to him, "I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary: The chapter is bracketed by "I am the LORD." Before any promise, God names himself. The ground of every "I will" is the unchanging "I am." Our hope rests not first on what God will do but on who God is.

verseByVerse.quote: I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I did not make myself known to them.
verseByVerse.commentary: A new depth of revelation dawns. The patriarchs knew God as El Shaddai; now the covenant name YHWH is unveiled in saving power. God reveals himself progressively, each generation receiving more of his glory — until the fullness shines in Christ.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God lays out the chain of redemption: I will bring out, deliver, redeem, take you as my people, be your God, bring you in, and give the land. Every promise is bracketed by "I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.theology: Salvation is monergistic — the work of God alone. Each verb belongs to God; Israel's role is to be brought, delivered, and taken. So too our redemption is God's doing from first to last.
verseByVerse.examples: These promises form the covenant heart of the gospel: "I will be your God, and you shall be my people" — echoed in Jeremiah's new covenant and fulfilled in Revelation 21:3.

verseByVerse.quote: Say therefore to the people of Israel, 'I am the LORD, and I will bring you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians, and I will deliver you from slavery to them, and I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary: The word "redeem" (ga'al) means to buy back as a kinsman-redeemer. God acts as Israel's near kinsman. The "outstretched arm" becomes the signature of his saving power — fully extended at Calvary, where Christ our Redeemer is stretched out for us.

verseByVerse.quote: I will take you to be my people, and I will be your God, and you shall know that I am the LORD your God, who has brought you out from under the burdens of the Egyptians.
verseByVerse.commentary: The covenant formula in its purest form. The goal of redemption is relationship: "my people" and "your God." Keller notes this is the deepest human longing — to belong wholly to God and have God belong wholly to us — and it is the very thing redemption secures.

verseByVerse.quote: I will bring you into the land that I swore to give to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob. I will give it to you for a possession. I am the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary: The promise reaches its goal: the land, sworn to the fathers. Redemption is never merely rescue from; it is always rescue into — into a possession, an inheritance, a home. So our redemption in Christ secures an inheritance kept in heaven for us (1 Pet. 1:4).

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses said to the LORD, "Behold, the people of Israel have not listened to me. How then shall Pharaoh listen to me, one of uncircumcised lips?"
verseByVerse.commentary: Even after the magnificent "I wills," Moses returns to his weakness. Carson notes that the persistence of human frailty only magnifies the sufficiency of God, who accomplishes his purpose through unwilling and faltering servants.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 9-30 — Unbelief, Genealogy, and a Reluctant Mediator
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people do not listen because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery. A genealogy establishes the lineage of Moses and Aaron, and Moses again protests his "uncircumcised lips."
verseByVerse.theology: God's promises stand even when his people cannot believe them. The genealogy roots redemption in real history and real, flawed people whom God nonetheless uses.
verseByVerse.examples: Even great mediators are weak vessels. Moses' faltering points us to the one Mediator whose lips never faltered and whose obedience never failed.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke thus to the people of Israel, but they did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary: Sometimes suffering so crushes the spirit that even good news cannot penetrate. God's promise does not depend on their reception of it. He will deliver a people too beaten to believe — grace that runs ahead of faith.

verseByVerse.quote: I will redeem you with an outstretched arm and with great acts of judgment.
verseByVerse.commentary: The "outstretched arm" recurs as the signature of God's saving might. Isaiah will ask, "To whom has the arm of the LORD been revealed?" (Isa. 53:1) — and answer with the Suffering Servant. The arm fully outstretched is Christ crucified, redeeming us at the cost of himself.

verseByVerse.quote: But the LORD said to Moses, Now you shall see what I will do to Pharaoh; for with a strong hand he will send them out, and with a strong hand he will drive them out of his land.
verseByVerse.commentary: God's answer to Moses' lament is not explanation but promise — and not just any promise, but the covenant name. I am the LORD. I appeared to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob as God Almighty, but by my name the LORD I did not make myself known to them. The patriarchs knew God as El Shaddai — the God who is enough, the God of sustaining provision. Now God reveals himself as YHWH — the God who acts in history, who keeps his covenant through time, who has not forgotten what he swore. The difference is not a new God but a new depth of knowing the same God. Every generation learns more of who God is by seeing him act.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses spoke thus to the people of Israel, but they did not listen to Moses, because of their broken spirit and harsh slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary: The people cannot hear the promise because the suffering is too loud. Broken spirit — literally shortness of breath. Slavery has stolen their capacity to hope. This is one of the most compassionate verses in Exodus: God does not condemn the people for their failure to believe. He notes the cause. Kidner observes that there is a kind of suffering that temporarily disables faith — not through sin but through sheer exhaustion. The God who gave the promise will have to create the conditions for the promise to be heard. He is patient enough to do that.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the heads of their fathers' houses... These are the Aaron and Moses to whom the LORD said: Bring out the people of Israel from the land of Egypt by their companies.
verseByVerse.commentary: The genealogy interrupts the narrative to establish the pedigree of Moses and Aaron — Levi, Kohath, Amram, Aaron and Moses. The names anchor the story in covenant history. This is not a random deliverer appearing from nowhere; this is the son of Amram and Jochebed, from the tribe of Levi, from the family of Kohath. The redemption of Israel will be accomplished through specific people, in specific families, descended from specific ancestors. God works in history, through lineage, through flesh and blood. The Word will become flesh — and that flesh will have a genealogy too.

verseByVerse.quote: On the day when the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt, the LORD said to Moses, I am the LORD; tell Pharaoh king of Egypt all that I say to you. But Moses said to the LORD, Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips. How will Pharaoh listen to me?
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses' objection — uncircumcised lips — is the same objection of inadequacy he raised at the burning bush. The repetition is not carelessness; it frames the entire section between the two commissions and signals that God's answer will be the same: I will be with you, and my word will be in your mouth. The great acts of God in Exodus are accomplished through a man who is convinced he cannot do them. This is by design. If a great orator had led the Exodus, the glory might have been shared with human eloquence. God chooses a stammerer so the glory stays with God.

6.theology:
Redemption is God's work. The seven "I wills" make every verb of salvation God's own. We are brought, delivered, redeemed, and taken — monergism written into the exodus.

The covenant relationship. "I will be your God, and you shall be my people" is the goal of redemption — not just rescue from bondage but belonging to God.

God's faithfulness over our unbelief. The people cannot believe, yet God will save. His promises rest on his character, not our capacity to receive them.
6.examples:
Then: To a people too broken by slavery to listen, God spoke seven sovereign "I wills," pledging to redeem them with an outstretched arm purely on the basis of his covenant.

Now: When our spirits are too crushed to believe the gospel, the ground of our hope is not the strength of our faith but the faithfulness of our Redeemer. His outstretched arm — Christ on the cross — has already secured the "I wills" of our salvation.

7.title: The Battle of the Gods Begins
7.text: <sup>5</sup>"The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring out the people of Israel from among them." <sup>10</sup>...Aaron cast down his staff before Pharaoh and his servants, and it became a serpent. <sup>13</sup>Still Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said. <sup>20</sup>...all the water in the Nile turned into blood.
7.overview:
The plagues begin, and we must understand what they truly are: not random disasters but a systematic dismantling of the gods of Egypt. "On all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgments," God says (12:12). Each plague topples a deity — the Nile that Egypt worshiped, the sun, the livestock, life itself. This is cosmic warfare: YHWH versus the entire pantheon of the world's greatest superpower, and it is no contest.

The chapter sets the terms. Aaron's staff swallows the magicians' staffs — a sign that God's power consumes all counterfeits. Then the Nile, the very lifeblood of Egypt and an object of worship, turns to blood. The river that ran red with Hebrew infants' blood (1:22) now runs red in judgment. God repays in kind.

Threaded through it all is the refrain of Pharaoh's hardening and the divine purpose: "that the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD." The plagues are not merely punitive; they are revelatory. Even in judgment, God is making himself known.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Moses as God to Pharaoh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commissions Moses again, making him "like God to Pharaoh" with Aaron as prophet. He forewarns that he will harden Pharaoh's heart and multiply signs, that Egypt may know the LORD.
verseByVerse.theology: God ordains both the means (Moses and Aaron) and the end (Egypt's knowledge of the LORD). His hardening of Pharaoh serves the revelation of his glory.
verseByVerse.examples: God's purpose in judgment is always self-revelation. Even his enemies will be made to know that he is the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: The Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I stretch out my hand against Egypt and bring out the people of Israel from among them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The refrain "that they may know that I am the LORD" recurs throughout the plagues. Sproul stressed that the supreme purpose of the exodus is the glory of God — the vindication of his name before the watching nations.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "See, I have made you like God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron shall be your prophet."
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses becomes God's representative, Aaron his prophet. God works through ordered means and appointed spokesmen. The pattern anticipates the prophetic office that culminates in Christ, the Prophet greater than Moses (Deut. 18:15; Acts 3:22).

verseByVerse.quote: But I will harden Pharaoh's heart, and though I multiply my signs and wonders in the land of Egypt,
verseByVerse.commentary: God declares his sovereign hardening in advance. Romans 9 takes up this very theme. The hardening is just judgment upon a willing rebel, not the corruption of an innocent — and it serves the multiplication of God's wonders and the display of his glory.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — Aaron's Staff Swallows the Magicians'
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Aaron's staff becomes a serpent; Pharaoh's magicians replicate the sign, but Aaron's serpent swallows theirs. Pharaoh's heart is hardened.
verseByVerse.theology: The powers of darkness can imitate but never overcome the power of God. The swallowing serpent shows God's supremacy over all counterfeit spiritual power.
verseByVerse.examples: The enemy mimics God's works to deceive, but his power is always derivative and doomed. God's truth swallows up every counterfeit.

verseByVerse.quote: For each man cast down his staff, and they became serpents. But Aaron's staff swallowed up their staffs.
verseByVerse.commentary: A telling detail. The occult arts of Egypt can produce a counterfeit, but God's power devours it whole. Carson notes that Satan's imitations always serve only to harden, never to save. God's truth consumes every rival.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Pharaoh's heart is hardened; he refuses to let the people go."
verseByVerse.commentary: Here Pharaoh's hardness is described as his own refusal. Scripture holds together God's sovereign hardening and Pharaoh's culpable obstinacy without apology. Both are fully true: God ordains, and Pharaoh chooses.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-25 — The Nile Turned to Blood
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first plague: Moses strikes the Nile and it becomes blood; fish die, the river stinks, Egypt cannot drink. The magicians imitate it, and Pharaoh's heart remains hard.
verseByVerse.theology: The plague strikes at the heart of Egyptian religion and economy — the Nile was worshiped as a god and was the source of all life. God shows his lordship over what Egypt idolized.
verseByVerse.examples: The river of Hebrew infants' blood now runs with judgment-blood. God repays oppression in measure, yet his ultimate aim is that all should know he is the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses and Aaron did as the LORD commanded. In the sight of Pharaoh and in the sight of his servants he lifted up the staff and struck the water in the Nile, and all the water in the Nile turned into blood.
verseByVerse.commentary: The lifeblood of Egypt becomes literal blood. The god-river is shown to be no god at all. As Kidner observes, every plague unmasks an Egyptian deity as helpless before the living God.

verseByVerse.quote: But the magicians of Egypt did the same by their secret arts. So Pharaoh's heart remained hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary: The magicians can mimic the plague but not reverse it; their counterfeit only deepens Pharaoh's hardness. As Carson notes, the devil's imitations of God's works serve always to harden, never to heal.

verseByVerse.quote: And all the Egyptians dug along the Nile for water to drink, for they could not drink the water of the Nile.
verseByVerse.commentary: The worshiped river becomes undrinkable; Egypt scrambles for water on every side. The idol that promised life now yields only death — a parable of every false god that cannot finally satisfy or save.

verseByVerse.quote: Still Pharaoh's heart was hardened, and he would not listen to them, as the LORD had said.
verseByVerse.commentary: The hardening refrain. Scripture says both that Pharaoh hardened his own heart and that God hardened it — a profound mystery of divine sovereignty and human responsibility that Romans 9 takes up directly.
