verseByVerse.quote: Then Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a tambourine in her hand, and all the women went out after her with tambourines and dancing.
verseByVerse.commentary: The joy cannot be contained; it spills into music and dancing. Miriam leads the women in answering song. Salvation is not a private sentiment but a shared celebration — the whole redeemed community caught up in praise.

verseByVerse.quote: And Miriam sang to them: "Sing to the LORD, for he has triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider he has thrown into the sea."
verseByVerse.commentary: Miriam answers the men's song with the women's refrain — antiphonal praise rising from the whole community. The joy of salvation is too great for one voice; it must be answered, echoed, multiplied among all the redeemed.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses made Israel set out from the Red Sea, and they went into the wilderness of Shur. They went three days in the wilderness and found no water.
verseByVerse.commentary: From the height of song to the test of thirst — the redeemed life moves quickly from triumph to trial. The wilderness will prove whether the praise of the shore endures in the parched places. Faith must learn to sing in the desert too.

verseByVerse.quote: Pharaoh's chariots and his host he cast into the sea, and his chosen officers were sunk in the Red Sea... Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? Who is like you, majestic in holiness, awesome in glorious deeds, doing wonders?
verseByVerse.commentary: The Song of Moses is Israel's first great hymn. It is theology set to music: the acts of God celebrated, his character declared, his future purposes anticipated. Who is like you, O LORD, among the gods? This is not a question; it is a declaration that the question has been answered by what just happened. The gods of Egypt — Hapi of the Nile, Ra of the sun, Pharaoh himself who claimed divinity — have all been exposed as nothing before the God who parts seas and swallows armies. The song reaches forward to the conquest: terror and dread fall on Canaan; the LORD will bring his people in and plant them on his holy mountain. They are singing the end before they have lived the middle.

verseByVerse.quote: They went three days in the wilderness and found no water. When they came to Marah, they could not drink the water of Marah because it was bitter... And the LORD showed him a log, and he threw it into the water, and the water became sweet.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three days after the greatest miracle in their history, Israel complains about water. The transition is jarring and human. The bitter waters of Marah are their first wilderness test. Moses cries to the LORD; God shows him a log; the log sweetens the bitter water. Then comes the first wilderness law: if you will diligently listen to the voice of the LORD your God and do that which is right in his eyes... I will put none of the diseases on you that I put on the Egyptians, for I am the LORD, your healer. The physical healing of the water becomes the announcement of a healer-God. The early church saw the wood cast into Marah as a type of the cross — Christ the log that transforms bitter water into sweet, curse into blessing.

15.theology:
Doxology as the response to redemption. The redeemed sing. Salvation accomplished overflows into worship. Theology rightly ends in praise.

The incomparability and holiness of God. "Who is like you, majestic in holiness?" The song magnifies the unique, holy, warrior-King.

The everlasting reign of God. "The LORD will reign forever and ever." The exodus opens onto the eternal kingdom, fulfilled in Christ.
15.examples:
Then: Standing on the far shore with their enemies dead behind them, the redeemed people broke into the oldest song of salvation, exalting the warrior-God, majestic in holiness, who reigns forever.

Now: The proper response to redemption is song. We who have been brought through the waters in Christ join the song of Moses and the Lamb. Our worship now is the rehearsal of the eternal praise we will sing before the throne.

16.title: Bread from Heaven
16.text: <sup>4</sup>Then the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you..." <sup>15</sup>...It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat. <sup>18</sup>...whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack. Each of them gathered as much as he could eat. <sup>35</sup>The people of Israel ate the manna forty years, till they came to a habitable land.
16.overview:
Barely a month out of Egypt, the redeemed people grumble — not against Pharaoh now, but against God, even wishing they had died in Egypt where at least there was bread. The human heart, even the redeemed heart, is prone to forget grace and crave the security of its old slavery. Yet God responds not with judgment but with mercy: he rains "bread from heaven."

The manna is a daily miracle of provision and a daily lesson in dependence. It must be gathered each morning; it cannot be hoarded; what is kept overnight breeds worms — except on the day before the Sabbath, when a double portion keeps. God teaches his people to trust him one day at a time, to rest on the Sabbath, and to learn that "man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of the LORD" (Deut. 8:3).

And then Jesus takes up this very manna in John 6: "I am the bread of life... your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died... I am the living bread that came down from heaven." The manna was a shadow; Christ is the substance. As Ferguson reflects, the daily bread of the wilderness points to the One who alone can satisfy the deepest hunger of the soul. We feed on him by faith, and we shall never hunger again.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the wilderness the people grumble against Moses and Aaron, longing for Egypt's food. God promises to rain bread from heaven and send quail, that they may know he is the LORD their God.
verseByVerse.theology: The redeemed are prone to forget grace and idealize their old bondage. Yet God meets even ungrateful grumbling with patient provision, to reveal himself as their God.
verseByVerse.examples: How quickly we forget past deliverances and crave the security of former sins. God's patience with murmuring people is itself a wonder of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: and the people of Israel said to them, "Would that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots and ate bread to the full, for you have brought us out into this wilderness to kill this whole assembly with hunger."
verseByVerse.commentary: Astonishing ingratitude — they romanticize slavery for the sake of full stomachs. Calvin observed that unbelief always exaggerates past comforts and forgets present mercies. The flesh would rather have bread in bondage than freedom with faith.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Quail come in the evening and manna in the morning. The people gather it daily; each has enough, none has lack, and it cannot be stored overnight without spoiling.
verseByVerse.theology: God provides daily bread to teach daily dependence. The equalizing of much and little teaches contentment and trust in God's sufficiency rather than hoarding.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul applies the equity of the manna to Christian generosity (2 Cor. 8:15). God's people are to trust him for each day and share with one another.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day, that I may test them, whether they will walk in my law or not."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Bread from heaven" — the very phrase Jesus claims in John 6. The daily gathering is a test of trust. Will they depend on God for each day's portion? So we pray, "Give us this day our daily bread," learning the same dependence.

verseByVerse.quote: I have heard the grumbling of the people of Israel. Say to them, 'At twilight you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread, then you shall know that I am the LORD your God.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Even the provision answers the great refrain: "that you may know that I am the LORD." God feeds his people not merely to fill their stomachs but to reveal himself. Every mercy is a means of knowing God.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said, "...your grumbling is not against us but against the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary: To grumble against God's servants is to grumble against God. Murmuring is not a small sin; it is unbelief aimed at heaven. The redeemed are called to trust, not to complain against the God who saved them.

verseByVerse.quote: When the people of Israel saw it, they said to one another, "What is it?" For they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them, "It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat."
verseByVerse.commentary: "Manna" means literally "What is it?" — a mystery bread from heaven. Jesus declares the answer: he himself is the true bread (John 6:32-35). The wilderness manna sustained the body for a day; Christ, the living bread, gives eternal life. He is the answer to "What is it?"

verseByVerse.quote: But when they measured it with an omer, whoever gathered much had nothing left over, and whoever gathered little had no lack.
verseByVerse.commentary: Paul cites this very verse on Christian generosity (2 Cor. 8:15): in God's economy, abundance and need are balanced by sharing. The manna teaches both daily trust and open-handed care for one another.

verseByVerse.quote: Morning by morning they gathered it, each as much as he could eat; but when the sun grew hot, it melted.
verseByVerse.commentary: The manna could not be hoarded; it had to be gathered fresh each day. So grace is received daily, not stockpiled. Yesterday's manna will not feed today's hunger; we must come to God anew each morning.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22-36 — The Sabbath Provision and a Memorial
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the sixth day a double portion comes and keeps over the Sabbath, when no manna falls. Some disobey and find none. A jar of manna is kept as a memorial of God's provision throughout the generations.
verseByVerse.theology: God builds Sabbath rest into the rhythm of provision, teaching trust and rest in him. The preserved manna memorializes his faithful care.
verseByVerse.examples: The Sabbath principle of rest and trust endures; we labor and rest in dependence on God, who provides all we need. The preserved manna anticipates Christ, our enduring bread.

verseByVerse.quote: The people of Israel ate the manna forty years, till they came to a habitable land. They ate the manna till they came to the border of the land of Canaan.
verseByVerse.commentary: Forty years of unfailing provision — a daily testimony to God's faithfulness through the whole wilderness journey. The God who began to feed them did not stop until they reached the land. He sustains his people the whole way home.

verseByVerse.quote: And the whole congregation of the people of Israel grumbled against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness, and the people of Israel said to them, Would that we had died by the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt, when we sat by the meat pots and ate bread to the full.
verseByVerse.commentary: The second great complaint: hunger. Six weeks into the wilderness, the people are ready to trade liberation for full stomachs. This is not ingratitude born of comfort; it is desperation born of real hunger. The extraordinary aspect is God's response: he does not rebuke them but rains bread from heaven. Quail in the evening, manna in the morning — daily provision, never too much, never too little. God tells Moses: I will test them, whether they will walk in my law or not. The manna is not merely food; it is a curriculum. Dependence on daily bread from heaven is the shape of the covenant life. Jesus will teach his disciples to pray: give us today our daily bread — and will declare: I am the bread of life.

verseByVerse.quote: When the layer of dew lifted, there was on the face of the wilderness a fine, flake-like thing, fine as frost on the ground. When the people of Israel saw it, they said to one another, What is it? For they did not know what it was. And Moses said to them, It is the bread that the LORD has given you to eat.
verseByVerse.commentary: Manna — the word itself means What is it? — is the mystery-provision of the wilderness years. It must be gathered fresh each morning, except on the sixth day when a double portion is collected for the Sabbath. Those who try to keep it overnight find it rotten and wormy. Those who try to gather on the Sabbath find nothing. The manna disciplines the people into the rhythm of creation: six days of labor, one day of rest, daily dependence on God for sustenance. Deuteronomy 8:3 will explain the lesson: he humbled you and let you hunger and fed you with manna, which you did not know, that he might make you know that man does not live by bread alone, but by every word that comes from the mouth of God. Jesus quotes this verse when Satan tempts him with bread in the wilderness.

16.theology:
The grumbling heart and patient grace. The redeemed forget grace and idealize bondage, yet God answers murmuring with merciful provision.

Daily dependence. The manna teaches trust for each day, contentment, Sabbath rest, and the truth that man lives by every word of God.

Christ the bread of life. The manna is fulfilled in Jesus (John 6), the living bread from heaven who alone satisfies the soul's hunger forever.
16.examples:
Then: When the redeemed grumbled and longed for Egypt's bread, God rained manna from heaven, feeding them daily for forty years and teaching them to depend on him one day at a time.

Now: We still crave the security of our old slaveries and forget past mercies. God still calls us to daily dependence — "give us this day our daily bread" — and offers us himself, the true bread from heaven. Feeding on Christ by faith, we shall never hunger.

17.title: The Rock and the Uplifted Hands
17.text: <sup>6</sup>"Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people will drink." And Moses did so, in the sight of the elders of Israel. <sup>11</sup>Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed. <sup>15</sup>And Moses built an altar and called the name of it, The LORD Is My Banner.
17.overview:
Two scenes, both pointing to Christ. First, the people thirst and quarrel, testing God: "Is the LORD among us or not?" God commands Moses to strike a rock at Horeb, and water gushes out to give the people life. Paul interprets it unmistakably: "they drank from the spiritual Rock that followed them, and the Rock was Christ" (1 Cor. 10:4). The Rock must be struck for the water of life to flow — and at Calvary, Christ our Rock was struck by the rod of God's judgment, that the living water of the Spirit might pour out to a thirsting people. Strikingly, God says, "I will stand before you there on the rock" — God himself takes the place of judgment as the rock is struck.

Second, Amalek attacks, and as long as Moses holds up his hands, Israel prevails; when his hands grow weary, Israel falters — so Aaron and Hur hold up his hands until sunset. Here is a picture of intercession: the battle below is won by the uplifted hands above. Moses the mediator, with arms outstretched, prevails for his people — prefiguring the greater Mediator whose arms were outstretched on a cross and who "always lives to make intercession" for us (Heb. 7:25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-7 — Water from the Struck Rock
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Rephidim the people thirst and quarrel with Moses, testing whether the LORD is among them. God stands on the rock at Horeb; Moses strikes it, and water flows. The place is named Massah and Meribah.
verseByVerse.theology: The people's testing of God is unbelief; yet God graciously provides life-giving water from a struck rock. The striking of the rock is the means of the water.
verseByVerse.examples: The Rock is Christ (1 Cor. 10:4), struck by God's judgment that the living water of salvation might flow to a thirsting people. "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink" (John 7:37).

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock at Horeb, and you shall strike the rock, and water shall come out of it, and the people will drink." And Moses did so, in the sight of the elders of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: Astonishing: God says "I will stand before you... on the rock" as it is struck. The blow that brings water falls, as it were, where God himself stands. Sproul saw here a shadow of the cross, where the rod of divine justice fell upon God incarnate, that the water of life might flow to us.

verseByVerse.quote: All the congregation of the people of Israel moved on from the wilderness of Sin by stages, according to the commandment of the LORD, and camped at Rephidim, but there was no water for the people to drink.
verseByVerse.commentary: They camp where God commanded — and find no water. Obedience does not guarantee ease. God sometimes leads his people into thirsty places to teach them that he, not the circumstances, is their supply.

verseByVerse.quote: And he called the name of the place Massah and Meribah, because of the quarreling of the people of Israel, and because they tested the LORD by saying, "Is the LORD among us or not?"
verseByVerse.commentary: "Is the LORD among us or not?" — the question of unbelief in the face of mountains of evidence. Hebrews 3 warns us not to harden our hearts as at Meribah. The redeemed must beware the rebellion that doubts God's presence despite his proven faithfulness.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Pass on before the people, taking with you some of the elders of Israel, and take in your hand the staff with which you struck the Nile, and go."
verseByVerse.commentary: The same staff that struck the Nile in judgment now brings water in mercy. The instrument of judgment becomes the means of grace — as the cross, an instrument of death, becomes the fountain of life.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8-13 — The Uplifted Hands and the Battle with Amalek
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Amalek attacks. Joshua fights below while Moses holds up the staff of God on the hill. When his hands are up, Israel prevails; Aaron and Hur hold up his weary hands until sunset, and Israel wins.
verseByVerse.theology: The victory is won not merely by the sword below but by the uplifted hands above — a picture of prevailing intercession and dependence on God's power.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses' outstretched arms prefigure Christ, our great Intercessor with arms stretched out on the cross, who ever lives to pray for us (Heb. 7:25). The church wins its battles on its knees.

verseByVerse.quote: Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed.
verseByVerse.commentary: The outcome of the battle hangs on the uplifted hands. Begg notes this is a vivid parable of intercession: the real battle is fought in prayer. The hands lifted to God determine the victory of the people below.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses said to Joshua, "Choose for us men, and go out and fight with Amalek. Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand."
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua fights below while Moses intercedes above — the work of the church in two hands: faithful labor and prevailing prayer. Neither alone wins the day; the battle is won where action and intercession meet.

verseByVerse.quote: But Moses' hands grew weary, so they took a stone and put it under him, and he sat on it, while Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one on one side, and the other on the other side. So his hands were steady until the going down of the sun.
verseByVerse.commentary: Even the mediator grows weary and needs support — a beautiful picture of bearing one another's burdens. Yet it also points beyond Moses to the Mediator whose hands never grow weary, who ever lives to intercede. The church is called to hold up one another's arms in prayer.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua overwhelmed Amalek and his people with the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary: The victory below is real, won by Joshua's sword — yet it depended wholly on the uplifted hands above. So our efforts matter, but their fruit hangs on the intercession of our great Mediator, who ever lives to pray for us.

verseByVerse.quote: saying, "A hand upon the throne of the LORD! The LORD will have war with Amalek from generation to generation."
verseByVerse.commentary: The enemy of God's people is the enemy of God himself, and the LORD pledges perpetual war against him. Our battles are his; the victory is sure, for the One on the throne fights for us until every foe is subdued.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14-16 — The LORD Is My Banner
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God declares perpetual war against Amalek and tells Moses to record it. Moses builds an altar named "The LORD Is My Banner."
verseByVerse.theology: God himself is the banner under which his people fight and the one who secures their victory. The war against his enemies is his own.
verseByVerse.examples: Our battles are the LORD's; we rally under his banner, and the victory is his. "In all these things we are more than conquerors through him who loved us" (Rom. 8:37).

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses built an altar and called the name of it, The LORD Is My Banner,
verseByVerse.commentary: The victory is credited entirely to God; the altar bears his name as banner. We do not fight for victory but from victory — rallying under the standard of the LORD who fights for us. The triumph is his, and so is the glory.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore the people quarreled with Moses and said, Give us water to drink. And Moses said to them, Why do you quarrel with me? Why do you test the LORD?
verseByVerse.commentary: The third great complaint: no water. The pattern is establishing itself — need, complaint, provision — but each iteration intensifies. At Marah the water was bitter; here there is no water. The people quarrel with Moses so fiercely that he cries to God: What shall I do with this people? They are almost ready to stone me. The escalation reveals the fragility of the people's faith but also the remarkable patience of God. He does not abandon them; he does not destroy them; he provides. Faithfulness meets faithlessness with grace, again and again, as it must — because the God who made the promise to Abraham cannot let the promise fail because of the people's weakness.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Amalek came and fought with Israel at Rephidim... Whenever Moses held up his hand, Israel prevailed, and whenever he lowered his hand, Amalek prevailed.
verseByVerse.commentary: The battle with Amalek introduces the theology of intercessory prayer as warfare. Moses stands on the hill with his hands raised; Israel prevails. When his hands drop, Amalek gains ground. Aaron and Hur hold up his arms until sunset; Israel wins. The interceding mediator, arms stretched wide, sustaining a people in battle through prayer alone — the image is impossible to read without thinking of the one who stretched out his arms on the cross. The victory over Amalek is to be remembered forever: write it in a book, recite it to Joshua. The memory of God's deliverance is itself a weapon against future enemies.

17.theology:
Christ the struck Rock. The rock struck for water (1 Cor. 10:4) is Christ, struck by God's judgment that living water might flow to thirsting sinners.

The ministry of intercession. Moses' uplifted hands win the battle below, prefiguring Christ's ever-living intercession and the church's call to prevailing prayer.

The LORD our Banner. The battle and the victory are God's. We fight under his standard and credit the triumph to him alone.
17.examples:
Then: God brought water from a struck rock to a thirsting, doubting people, and gave victory over Amalek through the uplifted hands of Moses, held steady by Aaron and Hur until sundown.

Now: Christ our Rock was struck that the living water of the Spirit might flow to us; he ever lives, with hands once outstretched on the cross, to intercede for us. And the church wins its battles under the LORD's banner, holding up one another in prayer.

18.title: Wise Counsel and Shared Burdens
18.text: <sup>11</sup>"Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods, because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people." <sup>18</sup>"You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone." <sup>21</sup>"Moreover, look for able men from all the people, men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe, and place such men over the people..."
18.overview:
After the great deliverance comes a quieter but vital chapter on leadership and community. Jethro, Moses' Midianite father-in-law, hears all that God has done, comes to Moses, and rejoices, confessing, "Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods." Here is an early fruit of the exodus among the nations — a Gentile priest worshiping the God of Israel. The mighty acts of God draw the watching world to praise.

Then Jethro observes Moses single-handedly judging the people from morning to evening and gives wise counsel: this will wear you out; the burden is too heavy to bear alone. Appoint capable, God-fearing, trustworthy men who hate a bribe, and share the load. The principle is profound for every leader and every church: ministry is not a solo performance but a shared calling. As MacArthur notes, the wise leader multiplies himself through others, raising up and entrusting godly people with real responsibility.

This is the seed of biblical delegation and the discipleship principle — the same wisdom that shapes the appointment of elders and deacons in the New Testament church. The qualifications Jethro names — fearing God, trustworthy, hating bribes — are deeply spiritual, not merely managerial. God's work must be done by God's kind of people.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jethro brings Moses' wife and sons and rejoices at all God has done. He confesses the LORD is greater than all gods, offers sacrifices, and shares a meal before God with Aaron and the elders.
verseByVerse.theology: God's mighty acts draw even Gentiles to worship. Jethro's confession and sacrifice are first fruits of the nations coming to know the LORD.
verseByVerse.examples: The deliverance of God's people is a testimony to the watching world. Our salvation is meant to provoke worship in those who observe God's grace toward us.

verseByVerse.quote: Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods, because in this affair they dealt arrogantly with the people."
verseByVerse.commentary: A Gentile priest confesses the supremacy of the LORD over all gods. The exodus was always meant to be a testimony to the nations (9:16). Here is an early harvest — a foretaste of the day when people from every nation will confess that Jesus is Lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Moses told his father-in-law all that the LORD had done to Pharaoh and to the Egyptians for Israel's sake... and how the LORD had delivered them.
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses recounts the mighty acts of God, and the telling leads to worship. Testimony to what God has done is itself a means of grace, stirring the heart — even a Gentile's heart — to praise.

verseByVerse.quote: And Jethro... brought a burnt offering and sacrifices to God; and Aaron came with all the elders of Israel to eat bread with Jethro before God.
verseByVerse.commentary: A Gentile offers sacrifice and shares a meal before God with Israel's leaders — a foretaste of the day when the nations stream in to feast at the table of the LORD. The exodus was always meant to bless all peoples.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jethro sees Moses judging alone all day and warns that he will wear himself out. He advises appointing capable, God-fearing, trustworthy men who hate bribes to share the judging, leaving only hard cases for Moses.
verseByVerse.theology: Godly leadership shares burdens rather than hoarding them. The qualifications for shared leadership are chiefly spiritual: fear of God, integrity, trustworthiness.
verseByVerse.examples: This is the seed of biblical eldership and the discipleship principle — raising up and entrusting godly people, multiplying ministry rather than centralizing it.

verseByVerse.quote: You and the people with you will certainly wear yourselves out, for the thing is too heavy for you. You are not able to do it alone."
verseByVerse.commentary: Even Moses cannot carry the whole burden alone. Begg notes that the refusal to delegate is often pride masquerading as diligence. Sustainable ministry requires shared labor; the leader who tries to do everything will ruin both himself and the people.

verseByVerse.quote: Now obey my voice; I will give you advice, and God be with you! You shall represent the people before God and bring their cases to God,
verseByVerse.commentary: Wise counsel directs Moses to focus on his irreplaceable work — representing the people before God — while delegating the rest. Even leaders must discern their priorities and not be consumed by what others can do.

verseByVerse.quote: If you do this, God will direct you, then you will be able to endure, and all this people also will go to their place in peace."
verseByVerse.commentary: Shared leadership preserves the leader and brings peace to the people. The refusal to delegate exhausts the shepherd and frustrates the flock. God's work is designed to be carried together, in peace.

verseByVerse.quote: Moreover, look for able men from all the people, men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe, and place such men over the people as chiefs of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens.
verseByVerse.commentary: The qualifications are character before competence: fear God, trustworthy, hate a bribe. MacArthur observes these anticipate the elder qualifications of 1 Timothy 3 and Titus 1. God's work is to be entrusted to God's kind of people — the spiritually qualified, not merely the capable.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses heeds his father-in-law's voice and appoints leaders to judge the people, reserving only the hard cases. Then Jethro returns to his own land.
verseByVerse.theology: Wise leaders receive counsel humbly, even from unexpected sources. Humility to listen is itself a mark of godly leadership.
verseByVerse.examples: The willingness to receive correction and counsel guards leaders from the pride and isolation that destroy ministries.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses listened to the voice of his father-in-law and did all that he had said.
verseByVerse.commentary: The greatest leader in Israel humbly receives wise counsel from his Midianite father-in-law. Humility to listen, even to an outsider, marks true wisdom. The proud leader who cannot be advised is on the road to ruin.

verseByVerse.quote: Jethro, the priest of Midian, Moses' father-in-law, heard of all that God had done for Moses and for Israel his people, how the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary: Jethro's arrival is a quiet marvel. The priest of Midian — outside the covenant, a pagan priest — hears what God has done and comes to Moses. He listens to the full account of the Exodus: all the hardship, all the deliverance. Then he says: Blessed be the LORD who has delivered you... Now I know that the LORD is greater than all gods. It is a conversion testimony. Jethro joins Moses in worship, offering burnt offerings and sacrifices to God. The Exodus was accomplished so that all the earth would know that the LORD is God — and here, in the first chapter after the sea crossing, a Midianite priest is the first Gentile to confess it.

verseByVerse.quote: The next day Moses sat to judge the people, and the people stood around Moses from morning till evening. When Moses' father-in-law saw all that he was doing for the people, he said, What is this that you are doing for the people?
verseByVerse.commentary: Jethro's wisdom is practical and structural: the people need judges at every level, not one man at the top doing everything. Choose able men who fear God, who are trustworthy and hate a bribe — distribute the burden. Moses listens and implements. The humility to receive counsel from a father-in-law — a Midianite, no less — is a mark of Moses' greatness. The structure of distributed leadership that Jethro recommends will prefigure the eldership of Israel and, eventually, the structure of the church. Wisdom about organization is not worldly pragmatism; it is faithfulness to the calling, which requires the leader to be sustainable for the long road ahead.

18.theology:
The nations drawn to worship. Jethro the Gentile confesses the LORD's supremacy — a first fruit of God's purpose to be known among all peoples.

Shared leadership and delegation. Ministry is a shared calling. Wise leaders multiply themselves through godly, qualified people rather than carrying every burden alone.

Character before competence. The qualifications for leadership are chiefly spiritual — fearing God, integrity, hating bribes — anticipating New Testament eldership.
18.examples:
Then: A Gentile priest worshiped the God of the exodus, then gave Moses wise counsel to share the crushing burden of leadership with capable, God-fearing men — and the humble leader listened.

Now: Our salvation testifies to the watching world and draws others to worship. And the work of ministry is shared, not centralized: God raises up qualified, godly leaders to carry the load together, and wise leaders humbly receive counsel and delegate the work.

19.title: The Mountain That Burned with Fire
19.text: <sup>4</sup>"You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself. <sup>5</sup>Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples... <sup>6</sup>and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." <sup>18</sup>Now Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire.
19.overview:
Three months out of Egypt, Israel arrives at Sinai, and the covenant is formally established. God's opening words are pure grace: "I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself." Notice the order — redemption first, then covenant; deliverance first, then law. God did not give the law so Israel could earn salvation; he saved them first and then called them to covenant obedience as the redeemed. This is the gospel logic that permeates all of Scripture: we obey because we are saved, not in order to be saved.

God's purpose is breathtaking: "you shall be my treasured possession... a kingdom of priests and a holy nation." Peter applies these very words to the church (1 Pet. 2:9). The redeemed are God's prized treasure, set apart to mediate his presence to the world. But to be near this God, the people must be consecrated, for he is holy. The mountain quakes, wrapped in fire and smoke; thunder and trumpet sound; the people tremble. Bounds are set so none may touch the mountain and die.

Here Sproul's great theme thunders forth: the holiness of God. To draw near to God is no light thing. The trembling at Sinai prepares us to marvel that in Christ we now "come to Mount Zion" with boldness (Heb. 12). The fire that terrified Israel is the same holiness that, in Christ, becomes our welcome.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At Sinai God recalls his deliverance — borne on eagles' wings — and offers covenant: if Israel obeys, they will be his treasured possession, a kingdom of priests, a holy nation.
verseByVerse.theology: Redemption precedes law; grace grounds obedience. God's purpose is to make a people his own treasure, set apart as priests to mediate his presence to the world.
verseByVerse.examples: Peter applies these titles to the church (1 Pet. 2:9). We are saved first, then called to holy obedience and priestly witness as God's treasured people.

verseByVerse.quote: You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself.
verseByVerse.commentary: The covenant opens with grace remembered. "I bore you... and brought you to myself." Ferguson notes the goal of redemption is not merely freedom from Egypt but nearness to God — "to myself." Salvation's destination is God's own presence.

verseByVerse.quote: Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine;
verseByVerse.commentary: "My treasured possession" — Israel is God's prized treasure, his special inheritance. Yet "all the earth is mine": he chose Israel not from need but from grace, that through them he might bless all the earth. We too are his treasured possession in Christ (1 Pet. 2:9).

verseByVerse.quote: and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation. These are the words that you shall speak to the people of Israel."
verseByVerse.commentary: A staggering vocation: the redeemed are to be priests mediating God's presence to the nations. Peter says the church now fulfills this (1 Pet. 2:9). We are saved to be a holy people who make God known to the world.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7-15 — Consecration for the Holy God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people agree to obey. God tells Moses he will come in a thick cloud so the people may hear and believe. They must consecrate themselves, wash their garments, and prepare for the third day.
verseByVerse.theology: To draw near the holy God requires consecration and cleansing. Approach to God is never casual; his holiness demands preparation and reverence.
verseByVerse.examples: We approach God now only through the cleansing blood of Christ, who consecrates us once for all (Heb. 10:10). Reverence, not casualness, befits worship.

verseByVerse.quote: All the people answered together and said, "All that the LORD has spoken we will do." And Moses reported the words of the people to the LORD.
verseByVerse.commentary: The people pledge wholehearted obedience — a pledge they will quickly break. Calvin notes the law exposes our inability to keep our own promises, driving us to need a Mediator who keeps covenant perfectly on our behalf. Sinai humbles human self-confidence.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Moses, "Behold, I am coming to you in a thick cloud, that the people may hear when I speak with you, and may also believe you forever."
verseByVerse.commentary: God comes in a thick cloud — revealing himself while veiling his glory, for sinners cannot bear the full sight. Even his self-disclosure is an act of mercy, accommodating his infinite holiness to our frailty.

verseByVerse.quote: And you shall set limits for the people all around, saying, 'Take care not to go up into the mountain or touch the edge of it. Whoever touches the mountain shall be put to death.'
verseByVerse.commentary: Boundaries are set around the holy mountain. The holiness of God is dangerous to sinners; they cannot approach unbidden and live. The barriers at Sinai prepare us to marvel that in Christ we now draw near with boldness (Heb. 12:18-24).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the third day, thunder, lightning, thick cloud, fire, smoke, and a loud trumpet announce God's descent on Sinai. The whole mountain trembles. The people are warned not to touch it lest they die.
verseByVerse.theology: God's holiness is overwhelming and dangerous to sinners. The terror of Sinai reveals the infinite gap between a holy God and a sinful people.
verseByVerse.examples: Hebrews 12 contrasts Sinai's terror with Mount Zion's grace: in Christ we draw near to the same holy God with boldness, because he has borne the fire for us.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Mount Sinai was wrapped in smoke because the LORD had descended on it in fire. The smoke of it went up like the smoke of a kiln, and the whole mountain trembled greatly.
verseByVerse.commentary: The mountain itself trembles before God's holiness. Sproul taught that the dominant note of Sinai is the terrifying otherness of God — his holiness that no sinner can approach unbidden. This is the God who is a consuming fire (Heb. 12:29), and we draw near only through Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: On the morning of the third day there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain and a very loud trumpet blast, so that all the people in the camp trembled.
verseByVerse.commentary: Thunder, lightning, cloud, trumpet — the whole creation shakes at the coming of God. The trembling of the people is the right response to the manifest presence of the holy One. Hebrews 12 contrasts this terror with the joy of Mount Zion, to which we have come in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself. Now therefore, if you will indeed obey my voice and keep my covenant, you shall be my treasured possession among all peoples, for all the earth is mine; and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.
verseByVerse.commentary: The covenant offer at Sinai begins not with demands but with memory. God reminds Israel what he has done: I bore you on eagles' wings. The metaphor is tender and powerful — the eagle that carries its young on its back so they cannot fall, that hovers over its nest to teach them to fly. From that foundation of grace, the covenant is offered: if you obey my voice, you shall be my treasured possession. The word treasured possession (segullah) means a personal treasure, a king's private jewel. A kingdom of priests — not just a nation with a priestly class, but a nation that mediates between God and the world. This is Israel's calling, and through the church, the calling of all who belong to God (1 Pet. 2:9).

verseByVerse.quote: On the morning of the third day there were thunders and lightnings and a thick cloud on the mountain and a very loud trumpet blast, so that all the people in the camp trembled.
verseByVerse.commentary: The theophany at Sinai is the most terrifying event in Israel's history: smoke, fire, earthquake, thunder, the mountain shaking violently, the sound of a trumpet growing louder and louder. The people stand at the foot of the mountain and tremble. The God of the burning bush has arrived at full revelation, and the holiness of God is devastating at close range. The boundaries around the mountain are not religious theater; they are the physical embodiment of the chasm between the holy God and sinful humanity. No one may go up to the mountain or touch it or they will die. Hebrews 12 will contrast this with Zion, the new covenant mountain — not the mountain that must not be touched, but the mountain of the living God, the city of the firstborn, where we have come in Christ. The terror of Sinai is not cancelled but transformed.

19.theology:
Grace before law. God redeems first, then gives the covenant. Obedience flows from salvation, never earns it. The whole gospel logic stands here.

A treasured, priestly people. God claims the redeemed as his treasured possession and a kingdom of priests — fulfilled in the church (1 Pet. 2:9).

The holiness of God. The fire, smoke, and trembling at Sinai reveal a holy God whom sinners cannot approach casually — driving us to the Mediator.
19.examples:
Then: Having borne his people on eagles' wings out of Egypt, God established his covenant at a mountain that burned with fire and trembled, calling redeemed slaves to be his treasured, priestly, holy people.

Now: We are saved by grace and then called to holy obedience as God's treasured possession and royal priesthood. The terror of Sinai reminds us how holy God is — and how amazing it is that in Christ we now draw near to that same God with boldness and joy.

20.title: The Ten Words: Law as Gift
20.text: <sup>2</sup>"I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. <sup>3</sup>You shall have no other gods before me." <sup>18</sup>Now when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning... they trembled and stood far off. <sup>20</sup>Moses said to the people, "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin."
20.overview:
The Ten Commandments — the moral heart of God's law — do not begin with a command but with the gospel: "I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery." The law is framed by grace. God speaks first as Redeemer, then as Lawgiver. The commandments are not a ladder by which slaves climb to freedom; they are the shape of life for a people already redeemed. As Keller often said, the law is not how we get saved but how saved people live in grateful love.

The commandments fall into two tables: the first four govern our love for God — no other gods, no idols, reverence for his name, the Sabbath; the last six govern our love for neighbor — honor parents, do not murder, commit adultery, steal, lie, or covet. Jesus summarized them all in love for God and neighbor. They are a gift, revealing both the character of the God who gave them and the path of true human flourishing.

Yet the law also has a deeper purpose. As Paul teaches, "through the law comes knowledge of sin" (Rom. 3:20). The perfect standard of the commandments exposes our utter inability to keep them and drives us to Christ, who kept the law perfectly in our place and bore its curse on the cross. The law is a schoolmaster leading us to Christ (Gal. 3:24). The thunder at Sinai is meant to make us run to the cross.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-11 — The First Table: Love for God
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God speaks the first commandments, grounded in his redemption: no other gods, no idols, no taking his name in vain, and the keeping of the Sabbath.
verseByVerse.theology: The first table governs our relationship to God — his exclusive worship, his proper representation, the reverence of his name, and the sanctification of his day. Right worship is the foundation of all righteousness.
verseByVerse.examples: Idolatry remains the root sin (Keller): the human heart is a factory of idols. The first commandments expose every rival to God's supremacy in our hearts.

verseByVerse.quote: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.
verseByVerse.commentary: The preamble is pure gospel. Before a single command, God declares what he has done. Sproul stressed that this grounds all obedience in grace: the indicative of redemption precedes the imperative of law. We obey the God who has already saved us.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall have no other gods before me.
verseByVerse.commentary: The first and foundational command. Keller observed that every sin is, at root, a breaking of the first commandment — putting something in God's place. The human heart is an idol factory; the gospel alone can dethrone our idols by giving us a greater treasure in Christ.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not make for yourself a carved image, or any likeness of anything that is in heaven above, or that is on the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth.
verseByVerse.commentary: The second commandment guards the worship of God from human invention. We may not fashion God after our imagination. As Calvin said, the human heart is an idol-factory; this command calls us to worship the true God in the way he appoints.

verseByVerse.quote: Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Sabbath is gift before duty — rest patterned on God's own rest in creation. It points forward to the rest we have in Christ, who says, "Come to me, all who labor... and I will give you rest" (Matt. 11:28). The redeemed are invited to cease striving and rest in God.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not take the name of the LORD your God in vain, for the LORD will not hold him guiltless who takes his name in vain.
verseByVerse.commentary: God's name represents his very person and character; to use it emptily is to treat the holy God with contempt. Reverence for God's name is reverence for God himself. We hallow his name when we honor all that he is.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-17 — The Second Table: Love for Neighbor
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The remaining commandments govern human relationships: honor parents, do not murder, commit adultery, steal, bear false witness, or covet.
verseByVerse.theology: The second table protects life, marriage, property, truth, and the contentment of the heart. Jesus deepens each to the level of the heart — anger, lust, greed.
verseByVerse.examples: The tenth commandment, against coveting, reaches the heart's desires, showing that the law is spiritual and exposes inner sin no outward conformity can satisfy (Rom. 7:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Honor your father and your mother, that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.
verseByVerse.commentary: The first command with a promise (Eph. 6:2). Honoring parents is the seedbed of all rightly ordered authority and society. The family is the first institution God established, and reverence for parents trains the heart to honor God.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not murder.
verseByVerse.commentary: Human life is sacred because made in God's image (Gen. 9:6). To murder is to attack the image of God. Jesus deepens the command to the root of anger in the heart (Matt. 5:21-22), showing the law reaches deeper than outward acts.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not commit adultery.
verseByVerse.commentary: Marriage is God's good gift and a picture of Christ and the church (Eph. 5:32). To break the marriage covenant is to defile a holy thing. Jesus extends this to the lust of the heart (Matt. 5:27-28), exposing our need for inner cleansing.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not covet your neighbor's house... or anything that is your neighbor's.
verseByVerse.commentary: The tenth commandment reaches into the heart, beyond outward acts to inner desire. Paul says it was this commandment that exposed his sin (Rom. 7:7). No one can claim to keep it perfectly — which is precisely the point. The law drives us to Christ.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18-21 — The Trembling People and the Mediator
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people, terrified by the thunder and fire, beg Moses to mediate, fearing they will die if God speaks directly. Moses tells them the fear is meant to keep them from sin, and he draws near to the thick darkness where God is.
verseByVerse.theology: Sinners cannot bear the direct presence of the holy God; they need a mediator. The law's terror reveals our need for one who can stand between us and God.
verseByVerse.examples: Israel's cry for a mediator points to Christ, the one Mediator between God and men (1 Tim. 2:5), who alone can bring us safely into God's presence.

verseByVerse.quote: and said to Moses, "You speak to us, and we will listen; but do not let God speak to us, lest we die."
verseByVerse.commentary: The terrified people beg for a mediator — and rightly so. Ferguson notes this cry anticipates the gospel: we need someone to stand between us and the holy God. Moses points forward to Christ, the better Mediator, who alone can speak God's word to us and our cause to God, that we might live.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses said to the people, "Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin."
verseByVerse.commentary: The terror of Sinai is meant to produce the fear of God that keeps us from sin. Holy fear is not opposed to grace; it is its companion. The trembling at the mountain drives us to the Mediator who alone can bring us safely to God.

verseByVerse.quote: And God spoke all these words, saying:
verseByVerse.commentary: The Ten Commandments are introduced with the weight of the whole narrative behind them: God spoke all these words. Not Moses, not a committee, not the accumulated wisdom of generations — God himself, from the mountain of fire. This is direct divine speech, and it begins not with a list of rules but with a declaration of identity and relationship: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt. The commandments are not a ladder to climb to God's acceptance; they are the charter of a people already redeemed. Obedience is the response to grace already given, not the means of earning it. The gospel comes before the law in the structure of Sinai.

verseByVerse.quote: I the LORD your God am a jealous God... showing steadfast love to thousands of those who love me and keep my commandments. Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary: The jealousy of God is not pettiness but covenant love: he will not share his people with rivals because he is fully committed to their good, and idolatry destroys them. The steadfast love shown to thousands stands against the judgment following sin — mercy is God's dominant mode, judgment is his strange work. The Sabbath commandment is grounded in creation (not just the Exodus): God rested on the seventh day, therefore so shall you. The weekly rest is the sacrament of creation, the declaration that human beings are not machines and that the world does not depend on our labor. We rest because God rested; we trust because he is trustworthy.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall not steal. You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor... Now when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and the sound of the trumpet and the mountain smoking, the people were afraid and trembled, and they stood far off.
verseByVerse.commentary: The commandments against stealing and false witness protect the fabric of community — property and truth are the foundations on which trust is built. Without them, society dissolves into exploitation and deception. The people's response to the theophany is the right response: fear and trembling. They stand far off and ask Moses to speak to them rather than God. Moses reassures them: Do not fear, for God has come to test you, that the fear of him may be before you, that you may not sin. The fear that keeps them at a distance and the fear that keeps them from sin are the same holy trembling — appropriate, necessary, life-giving. The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses drew near to the thick darkness where God was. And the LORD said to Moses, Thus you shall say to the people of Israel: You have seen for yourselves that I talked with you from heaven. You shall not make gods of silver to be with me, nor shall you make for yourselves gods of gold.
verseByVerse.commentary: The laws for the altar that follow the Ten Commandments are deliberately simple: uncut stone, no steps, no elaborate construction. The altar is not to be a monument to human craftsmanship; it is to be a place of meeting with God. The prohibition of steps is practical modesty: nakedness must not be exposed before the altar. The theology of simple worship runs throughout Scripture — God is not impressed by architectural grandeur. What he seeks is the humble and contrite heart that trembles at his word (Isa. 66:2).

20.theology:
Law framed by grace. The commandments begin with redemption ("I brought you out"). Obedience flows from salvation; the law is a gift to the redeemed, not a ladder to earn rescue.

The two tables of love. Love for God (commands 1-4) and love for neighbor (commands 5-10), summarized by Jesus as the whole of the law.

The law as schoolmaster. The perfect standard exposes our sin (Rom. 3:20) and drives us to Christ (Gal. 3:24), who kept it for us and bore its curse.
20.examples:
Then: From a mountain of fire God spoke ten words to his redeemed people, framed by the gospel of their deliverance — the shape of life with God — while the terrified people begged for a mediator.

Now: The law shows us both how to love God and neighbor and how far we fall short. Its perfect standard drives us to Christ, who kept it perfectly and bore its curse. We obey not to be saved but because we are saved — in grateful love to our Redeemer.

21.title: The Dignity of Persons Under God's Law
21.text: <sup>1</sup>"Now these are the rules that you shall set before them. <sup>2</sup>When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing." <sup>23</sup>"But if there is harm, then you shall pay life for life, <sup>24</sup>eye for eye, tooth for tooth..."
21.overview:
After the Ten Commandments comes the Book of the Covenant (chs. 21-23), the case law that applies the moral law to the realities of life in a fallen, ancient world. To modern ears these laws can seem strange, but read rightly they reveal a God deeply concerned with justice, mercy, and the dignity of every person — especially the weak and the vulnerable. As Carson notes, these laws are stunningly humane compared to the brutal codes of Israel's neighbors.

The chapter opens with laws about servants, and immediately we see God's heart: even bondservice is limited, regulated, and oriented toward eventual freedom. The seventh-year release for the Hebrew servant echoes the exodus itself — God's redeemed people must extend the freedom they received. The law protects servants from abuse, secures the rights of the vulnerable, and treats every human life as bearing the image of God.

The famous "eye for eye" principle (lex talionis) is not a license for vengeance but a restraint upon it — a principle of proportionate justice that limited retaliation in a violent age. The whole chapter teaches that human life and dignity are precious to God, anchored in creation in his image and pointing forward to the Redeemer who would give his own life to ransom ours.

sections.title: Laws Concerning Servants
sections.commentary:
The covenant code begins with the most vulnerable: servants. A Hebrew servant serves six years and goes free in the seventh — a built-in limit echoing the exodus and anticipating the year of Jubilee. Even within an ancient economy of debt-bondage, God orients everything toward freedom. The servant who, out of love, chooses to remain with a good master is honored with a permanent place in the household. Calvin saw in these provisions God's tender care that no person be ground down without recourse. The dignity of every image-bearer is woven into the law.

Provisions for female servants protect them from exploitation, securing their rights to food, clothing, and marital protection. In a world that treated such persons as disposable, God's law surrounds them with safeguards. The God who heard the groaning of slaves in Egypt will not permit his people to become careless oppressors.

sections.title: Laws Concerning Violence
sections.commentary:
These laws distinguish between premeditated murder and accidental killing, establishing the principle that human life — made in God's image — is sacred. Intentional murder warrants death; unintentional killing is treated with mercy and provision (the seed of the cities of refuge). Striking or cursing one's parents is gravely serious, upholding the fifth commandment. The protection of persons, including unborn life harmed in a struggle, reflects God's concern for the most defenseless.

The lex talionis — "eye for eye, tooth for tooth" — is widely misunderstood. As Carson explains, it is not a charter for revenge but a strict limit upon it: the punishment may not exceed the crime. In its context it was a profound restraint upon escalating violence and a guarantee of proportionate justice for rich and poor alike. Jesus later addresses its misuse as a personal excuse for retaliation (Matt. 5:38-39), calling his people to a higher righteousness of mercy.

sections.title: Laws Concerning Property and Responsibility
sections.commentary:
Even an ox that gores reveals God's justice: an owner who knew his animal was dangerous and failed to restrain it bears responsibility for the harm it causes. These laws teach personal accountability and the protection of the community from negligence. They presume a society where each person answers for the consequences of his actions and the welfare of his neighbor.

Underlying every statute is the conviction that we are responsible before God for our neighbor's safety and flourishing. The law refuses the modern fiction that what I do affects only myself. In God's economy, love for neighbor is not optional sentiment but enforceable duty — a foreshadowing of the love that fulfills the whole law (Rom. 13:10).

sections.title: The Heart of the Law: Mercy and Justice Together
sections.commentary:
Read as a whole, the Book of the Covenant reveals a God in whom justice and mercy are perfectly wed. The penalties are exacting because sin is serious and persons are precious; yet provision, limit, and mercy temper every statute. As Carson observes, these laws are strikingly humane against the backdrop of the brutal codes of the ancient Near East, where the powerful crushed the weak with impunity.

Behind every case law stands the character of the God who gave it — the God who heard the groaning of slaves and will not have his redeemed people become careless oppressors. The law is a mirror of God's heart, and ultimately a tutor that leads us to Christ (Gal. 3:24), who fulfilled its every demand and bore its every curse, that mercy and justice might embrace at the cross.

21.theology:
The dignity of the image of God. Every person — servant, child, victim — is precious because made in God's image. The law surrounds the vulnerable with protection.

Justice and its limits. The lex talionis restrains vengeance and guarantees proportion. God's justice is exacting but never cruel; it protects rather than oppresses.

Personal responsibility before God. We answer to God for our neighbor's welfare and safety. Love for neighbor is a real, enforceable obligation, not mere sentiment.
21.examples:
Then: God's covenant law applied his holy character to daily life, protecting servants, restraining violence, and upholding the dignity of every person in a brutal ancient world far harsher than its neighbors' codes.

Now: God still cares for the vulnerable and the oppressed, and still holds us responsible for our neighbor's welfare. His law reveals a God of justice and mercy — and points us to the Redeemer who gave his life to ransom ours, the ultimate proof of how precious human life is to God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the thunder of Sinai comes a book of case law — God bringing his holiness down into the dust of ordinary life: oxen, wells, quarrels, servants. He begins with the most vulnerable person in the ancient world, the bondservant. Hebrew servitude was not the race-based slavery of later centuries but indentured labor to work off debt, and God hedges it with mercy: freedom in the seventh year, protection for wives and daughters, dignity for the powerless. Already the gospel is peeking through — a servant who, for love, chooses to stay forever, and seals it at a doorpost with pierced flesh.
verseByVerse.theology: God's law reaches the servant first, because a society is measured by how it treats its weakest. The six-years-then-free rhythm is grounded in the exodus itself: Israel were slaves whom God set free, so they must not hold others in endless bondage (cf. Deut 15:15). Every limit here restrains the strong and shields the weak — the fingerprint of a God who "executes justice for the fatherless and the widow" (Deut 10:18).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a man drowning in debt could sell his labor, but never his humanity; the law guaranteed his freedom and guarded his family.

Now: we were slaves too — to sin, with no seventh-year release in sight (John 8:34). Then a Servant appeared who loved his Master and his bride and would not go out free, but gave his ear, his hands, his life, that we might go free forever (Rom 6:22).

verseByVerse.quote: When you buy a Hebrew slave, he shall serve six years, and in the seventh he shall go out free, for nothing.
verseByVerse.commentary: The very first case law protects the servant, and the sabbath rhythm rules even here: six years of labor, then freedom "for nothing" — no ransom required, the debt simply cancelled. This is astonishing in the ancient world, where a slave was property for life. But Israel's God had purchased a nation of slaves out of Egypt "for nothing," by grace, and their laws must echo that rescue. Notice too the tenderness over a man's family (vv.3-4): the law refuses to let servitude quietly swallow a household. Every clause is a fence around human dignity, because the servant, too, bears the image of God.

verseByVerse.quote: But if the slave plainly says, 'I love my master, my wife, and my children; I will not go out free,' then his master... shall bore his ear through with an awl, and he shall be his slave forever.
verseByVerse.commentary: Here is one of the most moving pictures in the law. A servant, offered his freedom, looks at his master and his family and says, "I love — I will not go out free." Love, not compulsion, binds him; and the choice is sealed forever at the doorpost, his ear pierced with an awl. Do you see whose face is in this? "Sacrifices and offerings you have not desired, but you have given me an open ear" (Ps 40:6); "the Lord GOD has opened my ear, and I was not rebellious" (Isa 50:5). Christ, the perfect Servant, looked on his Father and his bride and would not go free. He "emptied himself, by taking the form of a servant" (Phil 2:7), and let love drive the nails. The pierced ear at the doorpost points straight to the pierced hands at the cross.

verseByVerse.quote: When a man sells his daughter as a slave, she shall not go out as the male slaves do... he shall have no right to sell her to a foreign people, since he has broken faith with her.
verseByVerse.commentary: Now the most vulnerable of all: a poor father's daughter, sold in hardship. Far from licensing abuse, the law surrounds her with protections unheard of elsewhere — she may not be treated as disposable, may not be sold on to foreigners, must be given the full rights of a wife or set free without payment. Three provisions (food, clothing, marital rights) guard her, "and if he does not do these three things for her, she shall go out for nothing" (v.11). God legislates for the girl no one else would defend. This is the heart of the Lawgiver: he sees the unseen, and writes their dignity into stone.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-17 — Capital Crimes Against Life and Family
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The law now guards what is most sacred: human life and the family that shelters it. Murder demands the murderer's life — but God distinguishes the killer who "lay in wait" from the one into whose hand "God let him fall," providing a place of refuge for the accidental slayer. Then, striking or cursing a parent, and kidnapping a person to sell him, all carry the death penalty. Life is precious because it is God's image; the family is precious because it is God's ordering of society.
verseByVerse.theology: "Whoever sheds the blood of man, by man shall his blood be shed, for God made man in his own image" (Gen 9:6). The severity is a measure of the sanctity: to destroy a human life is to assault the image of God. Yet even here mercy is built in — the city of refuge for the unintentional slayer foreshadows the gospel, a place to flee where the avenger cannot reach. And that a man could be executed for "cursing" his parents shows how gravely God takes the fifth commandment, the hinge between honoring God and honoring men.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: the manslayer ran, heart pounding, to the appointed place, and inside its gates the avenger could not touch him.

Now: we are all under the sentence of a broken law, and there is one refuge: "we who have fled for refuge" to Christ, "might have strong encouragement to hold fast" (Heb 6:18). Run to him, and no accuser can drag you out.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever strikes a man so that he dies shall be put to death. But if he did not lie in wait for him, but God let him fall into his hand, then I will appoint for you a place to which he may flee.
verseByVerse.commentary: The law does not treat all killing alike. The murderer who "lay in wait," who planned and stalked, forfeits his own life — but the man who killed by accident, "God let him fall into his hand," is given a refuge to flee to (later, the cities of refuge, Num 35). Justice must be exact: it neither excuses the murderer nor crushes the unfortunate. And notice the mercy woven into justice — God himself appoints the place of safety. Here is the gospel in shadow: for guilty sinners under a just sentence, God appoints a refuge, and his name is Jesus. Even the altar (v.14) could not shelter the willful murderer — but the true altar, Christ, shelters every sinner who comes pleading his blood.

verseByVerse.quote: Whoever strikes his father or his mother shall be put to death... Whoever steals a man and sells him... shall be put to death... Whoever curses his father or his mother shall be put to death.
verseByVerse.commentary: Three crimes, one theme: the assault on persons and the bonds that hold society together. To strike or curse father or mother is not a private family matter but a capital offense, for the family is the first society God made, and contempt for parents is the seedbed of contempt for all authority, and finally for God. Between these two sits kidnapping — literally man-stealing, seizing a person to sell him. This is the very verse that condemns the slave trade the modern world would later build; God calls it a death-penalty crime (cf. 1 Tim 1:10, "enslavers"). The God who freed slaves will not tolerate the stealing of a single soul.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18-27 — Injury, Restitution, and the Limit of Vengeance
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: These verses handle bodily harm: a man injured in a quarrel, a servant struck, a pregnant woman hurt in a brawl. Here appears the famous phrase "eye for eye, tooth for tooth" — not a license for revenge but a leash on it. In a world where a bruised pride would take a life, God's law says: the punishment may not exceed the crime. And when a master maims his servant, that servant walks free — the powerful are held accountable to the powerless.
verseByVerse.theology: The lex talionis ("law of retaliation," "an eye for an eye") is one of the most misunderstood lines in Scripture. It is not permission to retaliate but a strict ceiling on penalty administered by judges — justice proportional, never runaway. Jesus does not abolish its justice; he forbids us to wield it for private revenge, calling us to absorb wrong rather than avenge it (Matt 5:38-39). And that a knocked-out tooth buys a slave's freedom (v.27) shows God weighing a servant's body as precious as a free man's.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a hot-tempered man learned that the court, not his own fury, would set the price of a wrong — and never more than the wrong itself.

Now: the cross is where justice was measured to the last drop — full payment made, not by us on our enemies, but by Christ for us. Freed from the ledger of revenge, we can "not repay evil for evil" (Rom 12:17).

verseByVerse.quote: When men quarrel and one strikes the other... if the man rises again and walks outside with his staff, he who struck him shall be clear; only he shall pay for the loss of his time, and shall have him thoroughly healed.
verseByVerse.commentary: God's justice is precise and practical. If a fight leaves a man bedridden but he recovers, the attacker is not executed but must pay for the lost wages and the full cost of healing — responsibility measured to the exact damage. The servant clauses (vv.20-21) are sobering to modern ears, but read them against their world: no other ancient code held a master criminally liable for a servant's death at all. Here the servant's life is protected by law, and the master who kills him "shall be avenged." The trajectory of Scripture, begun here, runs toward Paul's word to masters: treat your servants justly, "knowing that he who is both their Master and yours is in heaven" (Eph 6:9).

verseByVerse.quote: But if there is harm, then you shall pay life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, stripe for stripe.
verseByVerse.commentary: The case of a pregnant woman struck in a brawl gives us the famous "eye for eye." Feel first what it protects: the unborn child and the mother are so valued that harm to them demands strict account — early and eloquent testimony to the worth of life in the womb. Then the principle: lex talionis, "eye for eye." This is not a green light for revenge but a red light on it — the penalty a court imposes may never exceed the injury. In a vengeful world that answered a slap with a sword, this was mercy. Jesus later forbids us to use it privately, to trade blow for blow (Matt 5:38-39); yet at the cross its justice was fully honored — "stripe for stripe," our wounds laid on him, "with his wounds we are healed" (Isa 53:5).

verseByVerse.quote: When a man strikes the eye of his slave... and destroys it, he shall let the slave go free because of his eye. If he knocks out the tooth of his slave... he shall let the slave go free because of his tooth.
verseByVerse.commentary: Even a single tooth. If a master's blow costs his servant an eye or so much as a tooth, the servant walks free, compensated with the greatest gift of all — liberty. No ancient law dignified a servant's body like this. God will not let power abuse weakness without cost; the mighty are answerable to him for the small. This is the same God who notices sparrows and numbers hairs (Matt 10:29-30), and who will one day free every one of his own from every hurt, wiping away every tear (Rev 21:4).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 28-36 — The Goring Ox and the Responsible Owner
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter ends in the barnyard, with an ox that gores and a pit left uncovered. These homely cases teach a weighty principle: we are responsible not only for what we do but for what we let happen through negligence. The owner of a known-dangerous ox who fails to pen it is guilty of the death it causes. God's law reaches into fences and wells and warns: love your neighbor enough to guard him from your carelessness.
verseByVerse.theology: Responsibility before God is not limited to deliberate acts; it includes the harm we permit through negligence. The ox that had "been accustomed to gore" and was left loose makes its owner liable — a principle of foreseeable harm still at the root of justice today. Under God's eye, love for neighbor means active care, covering the pit, penning the beast, guarding others from danger we could prevent (cf. Deut 22:8).
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: a farmer who knew his bull was dangerous had a choice — build the pen or answer for the death. Negligence was no defense.

Now: the sins we most excuse are often sins of omission — the pit we never covered, the word we never spoke, the care we withheld. "Whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin" (James 4:17). Grace both forgives our negligence and frees us to cover our neighbor's pit.

verseByVerse.quote: When an ox gores a man or a woman to death, the ox shall be stoned... But if the ox has been accustomed to gore in the past, and its owner has been warned but has not kept it in, and it kills a man or a woman... its owner also shall be put to death.
verseByVerse.commentary: If an ox suddenly gores someone, the animal is destroyed but the owner goes free — it was not foreseeable. But if the ox was a known gorer and the owner, warned, did nothing to restrain it, the owner bears the guilt of the death. This is the birth of the legal principle of negligence: we answer for harm we could and should have prevented. God takes seriously the pen we never built. Even the goring of a servant is priced (v.32) — thirty shekels of silver, the very sum later weighed out to betray the Lord of glory (Matt 26:15; Zech 11:12), a chilling echo that the price of a slave was set on the Master of all.

verseByVerse.quote: When a man opens a pit... and an ox or a donkey falls into it, the owner of the pit shall make restoration... When one man's ox butts another's, so that it dies, then they shall sell the live ox and share its price.
verseByVerse.commentary: The uncovered pit and the fighting oxen round out the lesson: careless harm must be repaid, and losses shared with fairness. If you dig a pit and leave it open, the animal that falls in is on you — make restitution. If two oxen fight and one dies, the loss is divided justly between the owners. There is nothing too small for God's justice or too ordinary for his care. He who set the stars also cares whether you cover your well — because your neighbor might walk that way. The whole chapter has been teaching one commandment in a hundred practical shapes: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself" (Lev 19:18).

22.title: Care for the Vulnerable
22.text: <sup>21</sup>"You shall not wrong a sojourner or oppress him, for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt. <sup>22</sup>You shall not mistreat any widow or fatherless child. <sup>23</sup>If you do mistreat them, and they cry out to me, I will surely hear their cry..." <sup>27</sup>"...for that is his only covering... And if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate."
22.overview:
The covenant law continues with regulations on property, restitution, and social responsibility — but its deepest pulse is the protection of the vulnerable. Laws on theft and damage require not mere punishment but restitution: the wrongdoer must make the victim whole and more. God's justice aims at restoration, not just retribution.

Then the chapter rises to its heart with laws protecting the sojourner, the widow, and the fatherless — the three groups most defenseless in ancient society. And the motive God gives is the exodus itself: "You shall not wrong a sojourner... for you were sojourners in the land of Egypt." The redeemed must remember their redemption and treat the vulnerable as God treated them. Grace received becomes grace extended. This is the ethic of the gospel: "freely you have received; freely give."

Most tender of all is God's warning about the poor man's cloak taken in pledge: return it by sunset, "for that is his only covering... And if he cries to me, I will hear, for I am compassionate." The God of the burning bush who heard Israel's cry still bends his ear to the cry of the poor. As Keller has powerfully shown, concern for the marginalized is not a peripheral add-on to biblical faith but flows from the very heart of the God who redeems.

sections.title: Laws of Restitution
sections.commentary:
When property is stolen or destroyed, the law requires restitution — often multiplied. A thief must restore far more than he took. This is restorative justice: the goal is not merely to punish the offender but to make the victim whole and to teach the offender the weight of his wrong. Where the thief cannot pay, he himself is sold, that restitution may be made. Property is treated seriously because it represents a person's labor and livelihood, yet always in service of relationships rather than mere materialism.

These laws presume a community bound together in mutual responsibility, where wrongs are righted and trust restored.
