The dignity of skilled labor. There is no sacred-secular divide; artistry and excellence done for God's glory are Spirit-given graces.

The Sabbath as sign of grace. The Sabbath declares that God, not our labor, sanctifies us — the gospel embedded in the calendar, pointing to our rest in Christ's finished work.
31.examples:
Then: God filled Bezalel with his Spirit for skilled craftsmanship to build the tabernacle, and sealed the instructions with the Sabbath — a sign that the LORD, not human labor, sanctifies his people.

Now: God still equips by his Spirit those he calls to his work, dignifying every skill exercised for his glory. And the Sabbath still preaches grace: we rest because God has done the saving work. In Christ we find the soul's true rest — "come to me, and I will give you rest."

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-11 - Bezalel and Oholiab: Spirit-Filled Craftsmen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God names Bezalel of the tribe of Judah and Oholiab of the tribe of Dan as the master craftsmen for the tabernacle. He has filled Bezalel with the Spirit of God, with ability, intelligence, knowledge, and all craftsmanship.
verseByVerse.theology: The filling of the Spirit for artistic and craft work is one of the most overlooked but important theological moments in the Pentateuch. The first person in Scripture explicitly described as filled with the Spirit of God is not a prophet or a warrior but an artist. God's Spirit equips for beauty-making. The tabernacle, which is the dwelling place of God, will be built by Spirit-empowered craftsmen. The implication is profound: human creativity in service of God's glory is a spiritual activity, an act of worship, a Spirit-filled calling.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller observes that Bezalel's gifts — ability, intelligence, knowledge, and all craftsmanship — are the ordinary categories of skilled human work, and God fills them with his Spirit. This is the theology of vocation: the Spirit of God at work through human skills, in ordinary human categories of excellence, for the glory of God.

verseByVerse.quote: See, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, with ability, intelligence, and knowledge and with all craftsmanship.
verseByVerse.commentary: God names his craftsman: Bezalel, son of Uri, son of Hur, of Judah. The specificity of the call is remarkable — God knows this man's lineage and has chosen him for this work. The equipment is the Spirit of God: not just natural talent (though that is included), but divine empowerment for human skill. Oholiab of Dan — from the other end of the tribal spectrum from Judah — is given as his partner. Together they represent all Israel, all skill, all Spirit-given ability. They will not be working alone; God has given them all the able men with the skill to make the tabernacle. The church is built by many-gifted people, each one called by name, each one Spirit-equipped for their particular work.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12-18 - The Sabbath as Covenant Sign
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Even the building of the tabernacle must not override the Sabbath. The Sabbath is the sign of the covenant between God and Israel forever. Anyone who profanes it shall be put to death.
verseByVerse.theology: The Sabbath command is given in the middle of the tabernacle instructions as a deliberate interruption: even the sacred work of building God's house must stop on the seventh day. The Sabbath is not subject to exceptions, even for the most important project. The principle is that the Sabbath is itself the testimony — the living evidence — that Israel belongs to God. Work, even for God, does not define Israel's identity. Rest defines it: they rest because God rested, because God redeemed them, because they are not defined by their productivity.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul notes that the severity of the Sabbath penalty — death for profaning it — reflects the covenantal weight of the sign. To work on the Sabbath is to deny the covenant publicly: to say that human productivity is more important than divine rest. The seriousness with which God regards his own rest is a rebuke to every culture that cannot stop.

verseByVerse.quote: Above all you shall keep my Sabbaths, for this is a sign between me and you throughout your generations, that you may know that I, the LORD, sanctify you... It is a sign forever between me and the people of Israel that in six days the LORD made heaven and earth, and on the seventh day he rested and was refreshed.
verseByVerse.commentary: Above all — even above the building of the tabernacle — keep the Sabbath. The Sabbath is not one of many covenant signs; it is the sign, the testimony that Israel is a people set apart by God. The theological grounding is double: creation (God rested on the seventh day) and redemption (God sanctifies Israel). The rest of creation and the rest of redemption converge in the weekly Sabbath. The stone tablets given to Moses at the end of this chapter — written by the finger of God — contain the Law that the Sabbath seals. The covenant is complete: law, tabernacle, Sabbath, and the presence of God.

32.title: The Golden Calf and the Intercessor
32.text: <sup>4</sup>...he made a golden calf. And they said, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" <sup>11</sup>But Moses implored the LORD his God... <sup>32</sup>"But now, if you will forgive their sin—but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written."
32.overview:
While Moses is on the mountain receiving the law, the people commit the great apostasy. They grow impatient, demand gods they can see, and fashion a golden calf, declaring, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" Within weeks of the most stunning revelation of God's glory, they exchange the living God for an idol of gold. As Calvin observed, the human heart is a perpetual factory of idols; we cannot trust ourselves even for a moment.

God's wrath burns, and he threatens to consume the people and start over with Moses. And here the chapter rises to one of the most magnificent portraits of mediation in all Scripture. Moses stands in the breach. He pleads God's own glory and God's own promises. And then, astonishingly, he offers his very life: "if you will forgive their sin — but if not, please blot me out of your book." Moses offers to be damned for his people. He cannot actually accomplish it; but his offer points to the One who could and did.

For Jesus is the greater Moses, the true Mediator, who did not merely offer to be blotted out but actually was — who became a curse for us (Gal. 3:13), who was forsaken on the cross that we might be forgiven. Moses' intercession is a shadow; Christ's is the substance. As Sproul preached, the golden calf shows us the depth of our sin, and the intercessor shows us the height of God's mercy. The chapter ends with judgment and a plague, but the people are not destroyed — because a mediator stood in the gap.

sections.title: The Great Apostasy
sections.commentary:
While Moses delays on the mountain, the people demand of Aaron, "Make us gods who shall go before us." Aaron collects their gold and fashions a calf, and the people cry, "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt!" They even hold a feast "to the LORD" before it — a horrifying blend of idolatry and the worship of God. Within weeks of hearing God thunder "You shall have no other gods" and "You shall not make a carved image," they break the first two commandments outright.

The speed and depth of the apostasy is staggering. As Calvin observed, the human heart is a perpetual idol factory; left to ourselves, we cannot be trusted even for a moment. The golden calf is not merely an ancient sin but the perennial sin of the human heart — preferring a god we can see, control, and shape to our liking over the living God who shapes us. It exposes how desperately we need not only redemption but a new heart.

sections.title: The Wrath of God and the Intercession of Moses
sections.commentary:
God's wrath burns: "Let me alone, that my wrath may burn hot against them and I may consume them, and I will make a great nation of you." The sin is real, the wrath is just. But Moses stands in the breach and implores the LORD, pleading God's glory before the watching Egyptians and God's own covenant promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. "Turn from your burning anger and relent from this disaster." And the LORD relents from the disaster he had spoken.

Here is mediation in action. Moses does not plead Israel's merit — they have none — but God's glory and God's promises. The intercessor stands between the wrath of God and the people who deserve it. This is a shadow of Christ, our Mediator, who stands between us and the just wrath of God, pleading not our merit but his own finished work. That God "relents" in response to intercession reveals the mysterious power of a mediator's prayer and the heart of a God who delights to show mercy.

sections.title: Judgment and Moses' Offer
sections.commentary:
Moses descends, sees the calf and the revelry, and in righteous anger shatters the tablets — a vivid sign that the covenant has been broken. He burns the calf, grinds it to powder, and makes the people drink it. Aaron offers a feeble excuse. The Levites rally to the LORD and execute judgment on the unrepentant, and about three thousand fall. Sin against the holy God is no small thing; the covenant breach brings real and severe consequences.

The shattered tablets preach a sermon: the law is broken, and a broken law brings death. Yet judgment is restrained — the whole nation is not consumed. The tension between God's justice, which cannot ignore sin, and his mercy, which spares a people, builds toward its only possible resolution: a substitute who can satisfy justice and secure mercy at once. The chapter cries out for the cross.

sections.title: Blot Me Out of Your Book
sections.commentary:
The next day Moses returns to the LORD with the most astonishing intercession in the Old Testament: "Alas, this people has sinned a great sin. But now, if you will forgive their sin — but if not, please blot me out of your book that you have written." Moses offers his own eternal standing for the sake of his people. He cannot actually accomplish such an exchange — God answers that the one who sins will bear his own guilt — but the offer is a breathtaking foreshadowing of a greater Mediator.

For Jesus is the greater Moses, who did not merely offer to be blotted out but actually was — who became a curse for us (Gal. 3:13), who was forsaken by the Father ("My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?") that we might be forgiven and kept forever in the book of life. Moses' offer was a shadow; Christ's substitution was the substance. Sproul preached that here we see both the depth of human sin and the height of mediatorial love, all pointing to Calvary. A plague follows, but the people are not destroyed — because a mediator stood in the gap. And One greater than Moses would stand in our gap forever.

32.theology:
The idolatry of the human heart. The golden calf, made within weeks of Sinai, reveals that the heart is an idol factory (Calvin). We need not only redemption but a new heart.

The wrath of God against sin. Sin against the holy God is no small thing; the broken law brings real judgment. Justice cannot simply ignore rebellion.

The mediator who stands in the breach. Moses pleads God's glory and offers his own life — a shadow of Christ, who actually became a curse for us (Gal. 3:13) and was forsaken that we might be forgiven.
32.examples:
Then: While Moses received the law, the people made a golden calf, breaking the covenant almost before it was given. God's wrath burned, but Moses stood in the breach, pleading God's glory and offering to be blotted out for his people.

Now: Our hearts are idol factories still, and our sin against a holy God is grievous. But we have a greater Mediator than Moses: Jesus, who did not merely offer to be blotted out but was forsaken on the cross, becoming a curse for us. He stood in our gap so we would never be blotted out of the book of life.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: While Moses is on the mountain for forty days, the people pressure Aaron to make gods for them. Aaron melts their gold earrings and fashions a golden calf. The people worship it as the god who brought them out of Egypt. God tells Moses what has happened and proposes to destroy Israel and start over with Moses. Moses intercedes. He comes down and smashes the tablets. Three thousand die. Moses intercedes again.
verseByVerse.theology: The golden calf is the great apostasy of Israel — occurring while the ink of the covenant is still fresh, while Moses is still on the mountain receiving the tabernacle instructions. The irony is devastating: while God is designing his dwelling among the people, the people are replacing him with a cow they made themselves. The theology of idolatry is exposed here: idolatry is not atheism but the human demand for a manageable god, a god of our making who will go where we lead rather than lead where we do not want to go. The calf is given the credit for the Exodus — this is your god, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt. The redefinition of the Redeemer is the heart of idolatry.
verseByVerse.examples: Calvin writes: the mind of man is a perpetual factory of idols. The golden calf shows how quickly the human heart replaces the living God with something it can see and touch and control. Aaron's excuse — I threw the gold into the fire and out came this calf — is the pattern of every self-deception that follows idolatrous choices.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses said to Aaron, What did this people do to you that you have brought such a great sin upon them? And Aaron said, Let not the anger of my lord burn hot. You know the people, that they are set on evil. For they said to me, Make us gods who shall go before us... And out came this calf.
verseByVerse.commentary: Aaron's excuse is both the most pathetic and the most human moment in Exodus. He blames the people (they are set on evil), deflects his own agency (out came this calf), and avoids the direct question. He was the leader; he made the calf; he built the altar; he announced a feast to the LORD. Moses' intercession before God is one of the great intercessory prayers: Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants, to whom you swore by your own self. Moses puts God's own promise between himself and the destruction of Israel. God relents. Then Moses descends, sees the reality, smashes the tablets, grinds the calf, makes Israel drink its dust, and calls the sons of Levi. Three thousand die. Moses then returns to God: if you will not forgive, please blot me out of your book. The mediator offers himself for the people he is mediating for. The Son of God will fulfill this offer in a way Moses never could.

33.title: If Your Presence Will Not Go
33.text: <sup>14</sup>And he said, "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest." <sup>15</sup>And he said to him, "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here." <sup>18</sup>Moses said, "Please show me your glory." <sup>20</sup>..."you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live."
33.overview:
After the golden calf, the deepest question is no longer survival but presence. God offers to send Israel to the promised land with an angel — but to withdraw his own presence, lest his holiness consume this stiff-necked people on the way. And here Moses utters one of the most magnificent prayers in all of Scripture: "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here." Moses would rather have the wilderness with God than the promised land without him. He understands that the land without God's presence is no blessing at all.

This is the very heart of true religion. As Keller has said, the difference between a believer and a moralist is this: the believer wants God himself, not merely God's gifts. Moses does not want the milk and honey; he wants the God who gives it. "Is it not in your going with us, so that we are distinct... from every other people?" The presence of God is what sets his people apart — it is everything.

Then Moses dares to ask the unaskable: "Please show me your glory." And God answers with infinite grace and infinite reserve: he will cause all his goodness to pass before Moses and proclaim his name, but Moses cannot see his face and live. So God hides him in the cleft of the rock, covers him with his hand, and lets him see only his back. Sproul saw here both the unapproachable holiness of God and his astonishing condescension. We could never bear the full glory — but in Christ, "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6), we behold what Moses longed to see.

sections.title: The Threat of God's Absence
sections.commentary:
God commands Israel to depart for the promised land, flowing with milk and honey, and promises to send an angel before them. But there is a terrible catch: "I will not go up among you, lest I consume you on the way, for you are a stiff-necked people." The very holiness that makes God's presence the greatest blessing also makes it dangerous to a sinful people. When the people hear this disastrous word, they mourn and strip off their ornaments. The prospect of the land without God's presence is felt as catastrophe.

This is the crisis the golden calf created: the holy God cannot simply dwell among an unholy people without consuming them. The problem demands a solution that chapter 33 cannot yet fully provide — a way for a holy God to dwell with sinful people without destroying them. That way is found only in Christ, in whom God dwells among us in grace, having dealt with our sin at the cross.

sections.title: Moses' Prayer for the Presence
sections.commentary:
Moses pitches the tent of meeting outside the camp, and the LORD speaks with him "face to face, as a man speaks to his friend." Then Moses prays the great prayer: pleading for God's presence, he says, "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here. For how shall it be known that I have found favor in your sight, I and your people? Is it not in your going with us, so that we are distinct... from every other people?" And God grants it: "My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest."

Here is the heart of true faith. Moses would rather have the wilderness with God than Canaan without him. As Keller observed, the difference between a true believer and a mere moralist is that the believer wants God himself, not merely God's gifts. Moses does not crave the milk and honey; he craves the God who gives them. The presence of God is what makes his people distinct — it is everything. To have God's gifts without God himself would be the deepest poverty; to have God's presence in a desert is the greatest wealth.

sections.title: Show Me Your Glory
sections.commentary:
Emboldened, Moses asks the unaskable: "Please show me your glory." God answers with both grace and holy reserve. He will make all his goodness pass before Moses and proclaim his name, the LORD, declaring his sovereign grace and mercy. But "you cannot see my face, for man shall not see me and live." So God hides Moses in the cleft of the rock, covers him with his hand as his glory passes by, and lets him see only his back.

Here is the unapproachable holiness of God and his astonishing condescension held together. No sinner can behold the unveiled glory of God and survive; yet God graciously grants Moses a glimpse, sheltering him in the rock. Many have seen the rock that shelters Moses as a picture of Christ, our refuge from the consuming glory. And what Moses could not see — the face of God — is now beheld in Christ: "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6). In the incarnate Son, the glory Moses longed for has drawn near, veiled in flesh, so that we may behold it and live.

sections.title: The Crisis and the Cry: A Holy God and a Sinful People
sections.commentary:
The whole chapter turns on a single, unbearable tension: how can a holy God dwell among a sinful people without consuming them? The golden calf created the crisis; Moses' prayer presses it; God's reserve in revealing his glory deepens it. The land without God's presence is no blessing, yet God's presence among the unholy is mortal danger.

This crisis is resolved only in Christ. In him the holy God dwells among sinners in grace, because at the cross our sin was borne and atoned. The glory Moses could not see in full is beheld in "the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6). And the deepest cry of faith — "if your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up" — is answered forever in Immanuel, God with us, whose presence will never depart from his people.

33.theology:
The supreme value of God's presence. Moses would rather have the wilderness with God than the promised land without him. True faith wants God himself, not merely his gifts (Keller).

The problem of a holy God dwelling with sinners. God's presence among an unholy people would consume them — a crisis resolved only in Christ, who deals with our sin so God can dwell with us.

The unseeable glory revealed in Christ. No one can see God's face and live, yet in Christ we behold "the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ" (2 Cor. 4:6).
33.examples:
Then: After the calf, God threatened to send Israel onward without his presence, but Moses pleaded, "If your presence will not go with me, do not bring us up from here," and dared to ask, "Show me your glory."

Now: The mark of true faith is that we want God himself, not merely his blessings. "If your presence will not go, do not send me." And the glory Moses could not fully see has drawn near in Christ, the face of God among us. To have God's presence is everything; in Christ, that presence is ours forever.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: After the golden calf, God tells Moses he will send his angel but will not go with them himself — his presence would consume them. The people mourn. Moses meets God at the tent of meeting. Moses makes three requests: know your ways, go with us, show me your glory. God grants all three.
verseByVerse.theology: Moses' three requests in this chapter are among the most audacious and beautiful prayers in Scripture. The climax is the third: show me your glory. God's answer — I will make all my goodness pass before you, and will proclaim before you my name — is the definitive Old Testament self-revelation. The glory of God is not primarily light or power but goodness and mercy: I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy. God's glory is his grace. Paul quotes this in Romans 9 to establish the freedom of divine election. Sproul calls these the most important eight words in the Old Testament for understanding who God is.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson observes that Moses, who has just interceded for Israel after their greatest failure, now asks for more: show me your glory. Intercession leads him deeper into God rather than exhausting him. Those who stand in the gap for others are not depleted — they are drawn closer to the God they stand before.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses said, Please show me your glory. And he said, I will make all my goodness pass before you and will proclaim before you my name The LORD. And I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and will show mercy on whom I will show mercy.
verseByVerse.commentary: God's answer to Moses' prayer for the divine glory redefines glory itself. Moses expected light and magnificence — what he receives is goodness. The goodness of God passing before a man hidden in the cleft of a rock, shielded by God's own hand, is a declaration that the deepest attribute of God is not his power but his grace. But Moses cannot see his face — no one can see me and live. The back of God only, the afterglow of the divine passage. This is as much as any human being can bear of the unmediated divine glory. Until the Word becomes flesh and we behold his glory, full of grace and truth — and then even that fullness is graciously veiled in human form so that we can bear to see it.

34.title: The LORD, the LORD, a God Merciful and Gracious
34.text: <sup>6</sup>The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, <sup>7</sup>keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty..."
34.overview:
This is the high point of divine self-revelation in the Old Testament. Having asked to see God's glory, Moses is given new tablets and meets God on the mountain again. And God reveals his glory not first by sight but by proclamation — by declaring his name, his character: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness." This is who God is at the deepest level, the answer to Moses' prayer. The glory of God is supremely the glory of his grace.

This proclamation becomes the most-quoted text in the rest of the Old Testament, echoed again and again (Num. 14, Neh. 9, Pss. 86, 103, 145, Joel 2, Jonah 4, Nah. 1). It is Israel's creed about the heart of God. And notice the perfect balance: God is overflowing with steadfast love and forgiveness, yet "will by no means clear the guilty." His mercy does not cancel his justice; his justice does not quench his mercy. How can both be fully true? The answer comes at the cross, where, as Sproul never tired of saying, God is shown to be "just and the justifier" (Rom. 3:26) — where guilt is not cleared by being ignored but by being borne.

The covenant is renewed; God's grace triumphs over Israel's sin. And Moses comes down from the mountain with his face shining, radiant from being in God's presence — a glory Paul says is surpassed by the greater glory now shining in the gospel of Christ (2 Cor. 3). The God who is merciful and gracious has, in Christ, drawn infinitely near.

sections.title: The New Tablets
sections.commentary:
God commands Moses to cut two new tablets like the first, which he shattered, and to ascend the mountain again. As God's glory passes by, he proclaims his name: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty." Moses bows and worships, pleading for God to pardon and to go with his stiff-necked people.

This is the climax of divine self-revelation in the Old Testament. God answers Moses' request to see his glory not chiefly by sight but by the proclamation of his character — and the heart of that character is grace, mercy, steadfast love (hesed), and faithfulness. Yet held together with mercy is justice: he "will by no means clear the guilty." Here is the great tension of the gospel: how can God be both abundantly forgiving and perfectly just? Sproul taught that this tension is resolved only at the cross, where God is shown to be "just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Rom. 3:26). Guilt is not cleared by being overlooked but by being borne by a substitute.

sections.title: The Covenant Renewed
sections.commentary:
God graciously renews the covenant, promising to do marvels and to drive out the nations before Israel. He warns sternly against idolatry and intermarriage with the surrounding peoples, against making covenants with them or worshiping their gods, for "the LORD, whose name is Jealous, is a jealous God." He reaffirms the feasts, the firstborn, the Sabbath, and the firstfruits. The covenant broken by the golden calf is restored — entirely by God's grace, not Israel's merit.

The renewal of the covenant after such a grievous breach is a stunning display of mercy. Israel had forfeited everything; God restores everything. This is the pattern of grace throughout Scripture: not that we keep covenant with God, but that God keeps covenant with us despite our unfaithfulness. The warnings against idolatry remind us that grace is never a license to return to the idols from which we were rescued; the God who forgives is also the God who is jealous for the undivided love of his people.

sections.title: The Shining Face of Moses
sections.commentary:
When Moses comes down from the mountain, his face shines because he has been talking with God — so brightly that the people are afraid to come near, and Moses must veil his face. The radiance is the reflected glory of having been in God's presence. Even a glimpse of God's glory transforms and radiates from the one who beholds it.

Paul takes up this scene in 2 Corinthians 3, showing that the glory on Moses' face — though real — was fading, and was surpassed by the far greater and permanent glory of the new covenant. Under the gospel, "we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another" (2 Cor. 3:18). The fading glory of Moses gives way to the surpassing, transforming glory of Christ. To behold him is to be changed into his likeness — the radiance Moses reflected is now, by the Spirit, being worked into all who behold the glory of God in the face of Christ.

sections.title: The Name Above All Names: Grace and Justice Meet
sections.commentary:
At the center of the chapter, and of the whole Old Testament's self-revelation of God, stands the proclamation of the divine name: "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness... forgiving iniquity... but who will by no means clear the guilty." Here grace and justice stand side by side, both absolute, both true.

How can God be both abundantly forgiving and perfectly just? The chapter cannot yet say; the cross alone resolves it, where God is shown "just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus" (Rom. 3:26). Guilt is not cleared by being ignored but by being borne. And the glory of this name, reflected fadingly on Moses' face, now shines unfading in Christ, transforming all who behold him from one degree of glory to another (2 Cor. 3:18).

34.theology:
The glory of God is the glory of his grace. God reveals his glory by proclaiming his name: "merciful and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love." This is the most-quoted text in the rest of the OT.

Mercy and justice held together. God forgives yet "will by no means clear the guilty." The tension is resolved only at the cross, where God is "just and the justifier" (Rom. 3:26).

Transforming glory. Moses' shining face is surpassed by the greater glory of the gospel; beholding Christ, we are transformed from glory to glory (2 Cor. 3:18).
34.examples:
Then: God answered Moses' plea to see his glory by proclaiming his name — "The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious" — renewing the covenant after the calf and sending Moses down with a face shining from God's presence.

Now: This is the God we worship: merciful and gracious, yet perfectly just. At the cross his mercy and justice meet, for there our guilt was borne, not ignored. And beholding the glory of God in the face of Christ, we are being transformed from one degree of glory to another by his Spirit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-35 - The New Tablets and the Covenant Renewed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses cuts new stone tablets. God passes before him and proclaims his name: merciful, gracious, slow to anger, abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty. The covenant is renewed. Moses' face shines from being in God's presence.
verseByVerse.theology: The divine self-proclamation of Exodus 34:6-7 is the most quoted Old Testament text within the Old Testament itself — referenced in Numbers, Nehemiah, Psalms, Joel, Jonah, Nahum, and more. It is the bedrock confession of Israel about who God is. The balance of the declaration is essential: steadfast love and faithfulness (grace), but who will by no means clear the guilty (justice). God is not simply merciful; he is holy mercy. He forgives through justice satisfied, not through justice bypassed. The cross is the answer to the question Exodus 34 raises: how can a holy God clear the guilty? Through the Son who becomes guilty for the guilty.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg calls Exodus 34:6-7 the doctrinal spine of the Old Testament. Every time Israel or the prophets appeal to God's mercy, they are appealing to these words. When Jonah flees because he fears God will forgive Nineveh, he quotes these words. When Moses intercedes, he quotes these words. The whole story of Scripture hangs on these eight attributes.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD passed before him and proclaimed, The LORD, the LORD, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, keeping steadfast love for thousands, forgiving iniquity and transgression and sin, but who will by no means clear the guilty.
verseByVerse.commentary: Moses falls on the ground and worships. This is the right response to a declaration of God's character. He then intercedes immediately — please go with us, pardon our iniquity — using the very attributes just declared as the basis for his petition. God renews the covenant with warnings against idolatry and with the commands of the feasts. Moses spends forty days on the mountain, not eating or drinking. When he comes down, his face is shining from speaking with God, and he does not know it. The Israelites are afraid to approach him. He puts a veil over his face when he speaks to the people. Paul uses this in 2 Corinthians 3: Moses veiled the fading glory; but we, with unveiled faces, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another.

35.title: The Willing Heart
35.text: <sup>5</sup>"Take from among you a contribution to the LORD. Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring the LORD's contribution..." <sup>21</sup>And they came, everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him, and brought the LORD's contribution... <sup>29</sup>All the men and women, the people of Israel, whose heart moved them to bring anything... brought it as a freewill offering to the LORD.
35.overview:
After the dark chapters of the golden calf and the renewal of the covenant, the building of the tabernacle finally begins — and it begins with the willing heart. Moses gathers the people and calls for contributions, but not by compulsion: "Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring the LORD's contribution." And the response is a flood of generosity. Men and women alike, "everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him," bring gold, silver, fine cloth, precious stones, and skilled labor — so much that Moses will soon have to tell them to stop (ch. 36).

What a contrast to the golden calf! There, they tore off their gold to make an idol; here, they freely give their gold to build God's dwelling. The same wealth that fueled idolatry now fuels worship — when the heart is right. As MacArthur observes, true worship flows from a willing, stirred, moved heart, not from coercion or duty alone. God loves a cheerful giver (2 Cor. 9:7), and the building of his house is a community project of joyful, Spirit-stirred generosity.

Notice too the breadth of involvement: men and women, skilled craftsmen and weavers, leaders and common people — the whole community is caught up in the work. Bezalel and Oholiab are again named as Spirit-filled craftsmen who will also teach others. The tabernacle is not built by a few professionals but by the whole Spirit-led community, each contributing as their hearts move them and their gifts allow. This is the church at its best: a willing-hearted people, gifted by the Spirit, building together for the glory and dwelling of God.

sections.title: The Sabbath and the Call for Offerings
sections.commentary:
Moses first reminds the people of the Sabbath — even the great work of building God's dwelling must honor the rhythm of rest — and then issues the call for contributions: "Take from among you a contribution to the LORD. Whoever is of a generous heart, let him bring the LORD's contribution." He lists all that is needed: gold, silver, bronze, fine yarns, skins, oil, spices, and precious stones, along with skilled work for every part of the tabernacle. The work is comprehensive, and the call is to willing hearts.

That the Sabbath is mentioned first, even before the building begins, underscores that our work for God must never crowd out our rest in God. We do not earn his favor by ceaseless labor; we serve from rest, not for rest. The call for offerings is rooted in grace: God invites his redeemed people to give back from what he has provided, and only the generous, willing heart is sought.

sections.title: The Flood of Generosity
sections.commentary:
The response is overwhelming. "Everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him" brings contributions — men and women alike, bringing brooches, earrings, rings, gold, blue and purple and scarlet yarns, fine linen, goats' hair, skins, silver, bronze, and precious stones. The women spin the yarn with their hands; the leaders bring the precious stones. "All the men and women, the people of Israel, whose heart moved them... brought it as a freewill offering to the LORD."

The contrast with the golden calf is stunning. There, they tore off their gold to make an idol; here, they freely give their gold to build God's dwelling. The same wealth that fueled idolatry now fuels worship — for the heart has been turned back to God. True worship flows from a willing, stirred, Spirit-moved heart, not from compulsion. "God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Cor. 9:7). And the breadth is beautiful: men and women, leaders and common folk, the whole community caught up in joyful generosity for the house of God.

sections.title: The Spirit-Gifted Craftsmen
sections.commentary:
Moses announces that the LORD has called Bezalel by name and filled him with the Spirit of God, with skill and intelligence and knowledge in every craft, and has appointed Oholiab with him. Crucially, God has also "inspired him to teach" — the gifted are to equip others. The Spirit gives not only ability but the capacity to multiply ability in others, so that the whole community of craftsmen can share in the work.

Here is a beautiful picture of the church: a Spirit-gifted people, with leaders who not only exercise their gifts but teach and equip others to exercise theirs (cf. Eph. 4:11-12). The tabernacle is built not by a few professionals but by the whole Spirit-led community, each contributing willingly according to their gifts. This is the body of Christ at work — every member supplied by the Spirit, building together for the glory and dwelling of God.

sections.title: The Redeemed Community at Worship
sections.commentary:
The chapter paints a picture of the redeemed community at its best: a people resting in God (the Sabbath), giving from willing hearts (the freewill offering), and serving with Spirit-given gifts (the craftsmen). Men and women, leaders and common folk, the skilled and the generous — all are caught up together in building the dwelling of God.

This is the church as God designed it (Eph. 4:11-16): a body in which every member, gifted by the Spirit, contributes willingly to the common work, while the gifted equip others. What sin corrupted in the golden calf — gold torn off for an idol — grace now redirects to worship. The redeemed community gives, serves, and builds together for the glory and dwelling of God.

35.theology:
Worship from a willing heart. The tabernacle is built by freewill offerings from hearts stirred and moved by the Spirit, not by compulsion. "God loves a cheerful giver" (2 Cor. 9:7).

Redemption redirects what idolatry corrupted. The same gold that made the calf now builds God's dwelling. A heart turned back to God turns its resources to worship.

The Spirit-gifted community. Men and women, leaders and craftsmen, all contribute their gifts; the Spirit equips and the gifted teach others — a picture of the church building together (Eph. 4:11-12).
35.examples:
Then: After the golden calf, the building of God's dwelling began with willing hearts — men and women freely bringing gold, cloth, and skilled labor, so generously that the same wealth once given to an idol now built the house of God.

Now: True worship and generosity flow from a willing, Spirit-stirred heart, not from compulsion. The church is built when the whole community, gifted by the Spirit, gives joyfully and serves together. What sin once corrupted, grace redirects to the glory of God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses conveys the tabernacle instructions to the people. He calls for contributions of materials and skilled labor. The people's hearts are stirred and their spirits are moved — they bring more than enough. Bezalel and Oholiab are introduced to the assembly.
verseByVerse.theology: The people's generosity in bringing materials for the tabernacle is one of the most beautiful moments in the Exodus narrative. Everyone whose heart stirred him up and everyone whose spirit moved him brought the LORD's contribution. The heart stirring and spirit moving is God's work in the people — they give freely because God has moved them. This is the theology of covenant generosity: all that they have is God's gift; they return a portion as a glad acknowledgment of his ownership. The tabernacle is built by the people who were commanded to rest on the Sabbath — demonstrating that generous giving and rest are both expressions of the same trust in God's provision.
verseByVerse.examples: Keller observes that the tabernacle offering is the inverse of the golden calf. The people gave gold for the calf in a moment of fear and apostasy; now they give gold, silver, bronze, and fine fabric in a moment of joyful obedience. The same material generosity can serve either idolatry or worship. What matters is the direction of the heart.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came, everyone whose heart stirred him, and everyone whose spirit moved him, and brought the LORD's contribution to be used for the tent of meeting, and for all its service, and for the holy garments.
verseByVerse.commentary: The assembly hears the Sabbath command first — even the building of the tabernacle bows to the Sabbath — and then the call for contributions. The response is overwhelming: men and women alike, leaders and people, everyone whose heart was stirred. They bring gold jewelry, blue and purple and scarlet fabric, fine linen, goat hair, tanned ram skins, acacia wood, oil, spices, onyx stones. They bring their skills — the craftsmen, the spinners, the embroiderers. The community pours itself into the dwelling place of God, giving what they received from Egypt, consecrating the plunder of idolaters to the service of the living God. This is what the church has been doing ever since: taking what the world gave us and offering it back to God.

36.title: More Than Enough
36.text: <sup>5</sup>..."The people bring much more than enough for doing the work that the LORD has commanded us to do." <sup>6</sup>So Moses gave command... "Let no man or woman do anything more for the contribution for the sanctuary." So the people were restrained from bringing, <sup>7</sup>for the material they had was sufficient to do all the work, and more.
36.overview:
Here is one of the most delightful problems in all of Scripture: the people give so generously that Moses has to command them to stop. "The people bring much more than enough," the craftsmen report, and so "the people were restrained from bringing." When was the last time a congregation had to be told to stop giving? This is what happens when redeemed hearts overflow with gratitude — generosity becomes a flood that must be restrained, not coaxed.

The chapter then describes the skilled craftsmen, led by Bezalel and Oholiab, beginning the actual construction — the curtains, the frames, the veil, all made exactly according to the pattern God had shown. The work proceeds with painstaking obedience and exquisite skill, every detail conforming to God's command. The Spirit-gifted workers translate God's design into reality with reverent care.

As Ferguson reflects, generosity that must be restrained is the fruit of hearts captivated by grace. The Israelites had been slaves with nothing; now, having been redeemed and provided for, they pour out their wealth with joy. This is the gospel pattern: "You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Cor. 8:9). When we grasp how much we have received in Christ, our giving overflows. The building of God's dwelling is funded not by reluctant duty but by grateful, abundant, joyful love.

sections.title: Bezalel and the Willing Workers
sections.commentary:
Bezalel, Oholiab, and every skilled person "in whom the LORD has put skill and intelligence" set to work on the sanctuary. They come from their various tasks to do the work, and Moses gives them all the freewill offerings the people have brought. The work is a partnership: God supplies the skill, the people supply the materials, and the craftsmen supply the labor — all under God's command and design. Every part of the community has a role in building the dwelling of God.

The emphasis that God "put skill" in the workers reminds us that even our abilities are gifts of grace. There is no room for pride in service to God; the craftsman's skill, like the giver's generosity, comes from God himself. All the glory returns to the One who equips and provides. The workers are stewards of God-given gifts, deployed for God-given purposes.

sections.title: Restrained from Giving
sections.commentary:
Then comes the delightful problem: the craftsmen report to Moses, "The people bring much more than enough for doing the work that the LORD has commanded us to do." So Moses commands throughout the camp, "Let no man or woman do anything more for the contribution for the sanctuary," and "the people were restrained from bringing, for the material they had was sufficient to do all the work, and more." When has a congregation ever had to be told to stop giving?

This is the overflow of redeemed hearts. The Israelites, once slaves with nothing, now pour out their wealth with such joy that the giving must be restrained. As Ferguson notes, generosity that must be checked is the fruit of hearts captivated by grace. This is the gospel pattern: when we grasp the immeasurable riches we have received in Christ — who became poor that we might become rich (2 Cor. 8:9) — our giving overflows. The building of God's house is funded not by reluctant duty but by grateful, abundant love.

sections.title: The Curtains, Frames, and Veil
sections.commentary:
The construction begins in earnest. The skilled workers make the ten curtains of fine twined linen with cherubim, the coverings of goats' hair and skins, the acacia frames overlaid with gold set in silver bases, the bars, the veil of blue and purple and scarlet with cherubim, and the screen for the entrance. Every element is made precisely according to the pattern God had revealed on the mountain. The detailed repetition of the instructions, now in the form of execution, underscores the painstaking obedience of the workers.

The careful conformity to God's design teaches that worship is to be ordered by God's revelation, not human preference. Nothing is left to improvisation; everything is done "as the LORD had commanded." The beauty and precision of the work reflect the glory of the God it is built to house. And the cherubim woven throughout remind the worshiper that this is the threshold of heaven, the dwelling place of the God whom angels serve — all of it pointing forward to the greater dwelling of God with man in Christ and in the New Jerusalem.

sections.title: The Overflow of Grace
sections.commentary:
The defining image of the chapter is generosity that must be restrained. When have God's people ever had to be told to stop giving? This is the overflow of hearts captivated by grace — the gospel pattern of those who, having received much, cannot help but give much. The same hands that once tore off gold for a calf now give it freely for God's house.

Paul names the principle: "You know the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, that though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor, so that you by his poverty might become rich" (2 Cor. 8:9). When we grasp the immeasurable riches we have in Christ, our giving overflows. Generosity that must be restrained is the natural fruit of a heart that has truly tasted grace.

36.theology:
Generosity that must be restrained. The people give more than enough, until Moses commands them to stop — the fruit of hearts captivated by grace and the gospel pattern of overflow (2 Cor. 8:9).

Skill as a gift of grace. God "put skill" in the workers; even our abilities are graces, leaving no room for pride in service.

Worship ordered by God's pattern. Every element is made exactly as God commanded — worship is governed by his revelation, not human improvisation.
36.examples:
Then: The people gave so generously to build God's dwelling that Moses had to command them to stop, while Spirit-gifted craftsmen built every curtain, frame, and veil precisely according to God's pattern.

Now: When hearts grasp the riches we have in Christ — who became poor to make us rich — generosity overflows and must be restrained, not coaxed. Our gifts and skills are graces from God, deployed for his glory, and our worship is to be shaped by his revelation, offered with reverent, joyful care.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bezalel, Oholiab, and their team begin construction. The people's contributions exceed what is needed; Moses has to restrain them from giving more. The chapter describes the construction of the curtains, the frames, the bars, and the veil.
verseByVerse.theology: The restraining of generosity — Moses commanded the people to stop, for there was more than enough — is perhaps the most remarkable fundraising outcome in the history of religious giving. The people had to be told to stop. This is the overflow of Spirit-moved generosity: people who give from a stirred heart do not give until the obligation is met; they give until they are asked to stop. This is the picture of what giving for God's purposes should look like in every generation of the church.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson notes that the construction chapters of Exodus (35-40) carefully echo the instruction chapters (25-31) — everything is done exactly as the LORD commanded Moses. The obedience is precise and joyful. What God designed, his people build faithfully. The tabernacle is a monument to covenant faithfulness on both sides.

verseByVerse.quote: So Moses called Bezalel and Oholiab and every craftsman in whose mind the LORD had put skill, everyone whose heart stirred him up to come to do the work. And they received from Moses all the contribution that the people of Israel had brought for doing the work on the sanctuary.
verseByVerse.commentary: The construction of the tabernacle is described in almost identical language to the instructions — deliberate repetition signaling faithful execution. The craftsmen work exactly to specification: the curtains of ten pieces of fine twisted linen with cherubim; the fifty loops and fifty gold clasps; the eleven curtains of goat hair; the fifty bronze clasps; the frames of acacia wood, upright, with their silver bases. Every detail matters because every detail was given by God. The faithfulness of Bezalel and his team is a model of covenant obedience: not improving on God's design, not taking shortcuts, not substituting their own judgment for God's revealed will. This is what faithful stewardship of God's revelation looks like in practice.

37.title: Obedience in Every Detail
37.text: <sup>1</sup>Bezalel made the ark of acacia wood... <sup>6</sup>And he made a mercy seat of pure gold... <sup>7</sup>And he made two cherubim of gold... <sup>9</sup>The cherubim spread out their wings above, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, with their faces one to another...
37.overview:
This chapter recounts the actual making of the most sacred furnishings — the Ark and its mercy seat, the table of the bread of the Presence, the golden lampstand, and the altar of incense. What is striking is the repetition: nearly everything described in the commands of chapters 25 and 30 is now repeated in the language of fulfillment — "he made." God commanded; Bezalel made. The pattern shown on the mountain becomes reality in gold and acacia, exactly as God ordained.

This careful repetition is not tedious; it is theological. It declares that obedience matters in every detail. Bezalel did not improve upon God's design or add his own creative flourishes where God had spoken; he made it exactly as commanded. As Sproul taught, true worship is regulated by God's word, not by human invention. The Spirit-filled craftsman submits his considerable skill to the revealed will of God. Excellence and obedience go together.

And every object preaches Christ. The mercy seat, where God meets his people and the blood is sprinkled, is fulfilled in Christ our propitiation (Rom. 3:25). The bread of the Presence points to Christ the bread of life. The lampstand points to Christ the light of the world. The altar of incense points to the prayers of the saints rising through Christ our Intercessor. The whole sanctuary, built with obedient care, is a gallery of gospel portraits — every detail a finger pointing to the One in whom God dwells with us. Bezalel's faithful obedience in the small things is itself a form of worship.

sections.title: The Ark and the Mercy Seat
sections.commentary:
Bezalel makes the Ark of acacia wood overlaid with pure gold, with its rings and poles, and the mercy seat of pure gold with two cherubim of hammered gold at its ends, their wings overshadowing it and their faces toward one another, gazing down upon the mercy seat. The most sacred object is made first and with the greatest care — the throne of God on earth, the place where he meets his people above the blood-sprinkled mercy seat.

Every detail conforms exactly to God's command in chapter 25. The cherubim gaze down upon the mercy seat as if contemplating the mystery of atonement — "things into which angels long to look" (1 Pet. 1:12). The mercy seat, where the blood of atonement covers the broken law beneath, is fulfilled in Christ our propitiation (Rom. 3:25), the place where God's justice and mercy meet. Bezalel's faithful making of this object is the crafting of a gospel sermon in gold.

sections.title: The Table and the Lampstand
sections.commentary:
Bezalel makes the table of the bread of the Presence, overlaid with gold, with its dishes and vessels, and the lampstand of pure hammered gold with its branches, cups shaped like almond blossoms, buds, and flowers, and its seven lamps — all of a talent of pure gold. The exquisite craftsmanship reflects the glory of the God whose house this is. Beauty and excellence are offered to God, not as ends in themselves but as fitting expressions of his worth.

The table points to Christ, the bread of the Presence and the bread of life (John 6), and to the communion we have at his table. The lampstand points to Christ, the light of the world (John 8:12), and to the church called to bear his light. Made exactly as commanded, these furnishings declare that God's people live always in his presence, fed and enlightened by him. The almond-blossom design, recalling Aaron's budding staff, speaks of life and resurrection — the living light of God's presence among his people.

sections.title: The Altar of Incense and the Holy Oils
sections.commentary:
Bezalel makes the golden altar of incense with its horns, rings, and poles, and the holy anointing oil and the fragrant incense, blended as by a perfumer. The altar of incense, standing before the veil, is where the prayers of God's people rise as a sweet aroma before him. Everything is made according to God's precise specification, with reverent skill.

The altar of incense fulfilled in the prayers of the saints (Rev. 5:8; Ps. 141:2) reminds us that our prayers ascend acceptably to God only through the mediation of Christ, our great High Priest. The holy oil, used to consecrate the priests and furnishings, points to the anointing of the Spirit. Every object in this chapter, made in careful obedience, is a portrait of Christ and the worship he secures. Bezalel's obedience in every detail is itself an act of worship — a reminder that faithfulness in small things glorifies God.

sections.title: A Gallery of Gospel Portraits
sections.commentary:
The sacred furnishings of this chapter together form a gallery of gospel portraits, each one a finger pointing to Christ. The mercy seat is Christ our propitiation (Rom. 3:25); the bread of the Presence is Christ the bread of life (John 6:35); the lampstand is Christ the light of the world (John 8:12); the altar of incense is the place where our prayers rise through Christ our Intercessor (Rev. 5:8).

And every object is made in exact obedience — "he made it as the LORD commanded." Faithfulness in the smallest detail is itself worship. Bezalel's reverent craftsmanship teaches that we serve God on his terms, with our best skill submitted to his revealed will. The whole sanctuary, built in obedient care, declares the glory of the God who dwells with his people through the Christ to whom every detail points.

37.theology:
Obedience in every detail. Bezalel makes each furnishing exactly as God commanded — true worship is regulated by God's word, not human invention. Faithfulness in small things is worship.

Every object points to Christ. The mercy seat (Rom. 3:25), the bread (John 6), the lampstand (John 8:12), the incense (Rev. 5:8) — the whole sanctuary is a gallery of gospel portraits.

Excellence offered to God. The exquisite craftsmanship reflects the worth of the God whose house this is; beauty and skill are offered in his service.
37.examples:
Then: Bezalel made the Ark, mercy seat, table, lampstand, and altar of incense exactly as God had commanded, his Spirit-given skill submitted entirely to God's revealed design — every object a portrait of Christ.

Now: Faithful obedience in every detail is itself worship; we serve God on his terms, not ours. And the sacred furnishings preach the gospel still: Christ our mercy seat, our bread, our light, and our Intercessor through whom our prayers rise as sweet incense before God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-29 - Making the Ark, Table, Lampstand, and Altar of Incense
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Bezalel makes the ark with its mercy seat and golden cherubim, the table of the bread of the Presence, the golden lampstand, and the altar of incense. The anointing oil and incense formulas are prepared.
verseByVerse.theology: The making of the mercy seat is the climax of this chapter. The ark contains the Law; the mercy seat covers it. The cherubim face each other, their wings spread above, looking down at the mercy seat. Between the cherubim, above the mercy seat, is the presence of God. This spatial arrangement is the entire gospel in wood and gold: the Law is real and present (the tablets in the ark), but the mercy of God covers it and the glory of God rests above it. The Law does not have the final word; the mercy seat does. Hilasmos — the same Greek word for propitiation/mercy seat — is used by Paul in Romans 3:25: whom God put forward as a propitiation (mercy seat) by his blood.
verseByVerse.examples: Sproul writes that the mercy seat is the Old Testament's most precise picture of the atonement: blood sprinkled on the lid of the ark, between the Law and the presence of God, satisfying both justice and holiness. When Jesus is presented as our hilasmos, he is our mercy seat — the place where God's justice and God's mercy meet.

verseByVerse.quote: He made the mercy seat of pure gold. Two cubits and a half was its length, and a cubit and a half its breadth. And he made two cherubim of gold. He made them of hammered work on the two ends of the mercy seat... The cherubim spread out their wings above, overshadowing the mercy seat with their wings, with their faces one to another; toward the mercy seat were the faces of the cherubim.
verseByVerse.commentary: The mercy seat — kapporeth, the covering, the place of atonement — is beaten from a single piece of gold. The cherubim face each other, looking down at the place where blood will be sprinkled on Yom Kippur. They are witnesses to the atonement. Their wings spread above, creating a canopy over the mercy seat, echoing the wings of the cherubim that guard the tree of life in Eden. The lampstand of pure gold — hammered out, not cast, all of one piece, with seven branches and seventy ornamental almond blossoms — is the most beautiful object in the tabernacle. Seven lights burning, seven branches alive with golden flowers, the menorah that will burn through all the years of Israel's temple worship and beyond. Jesus will say: I am the light of the world. The lampstand bears his testimony before his coming.

38.title: The Altar, the Court, and the Reckoning
38.text: <sup>1</sup>He made the altar of burnt offering of acacia wood... <sup>8</sup>He made the basin of bronze and its stand of bronze, from the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered in the entrance of the tent of meeting. <sup>21</sup>These are the records of the tabernacle... as they were recorded at the commandment of Moses.
38.overview:
The construction continues with the bronze altar of burnt offering, the bronze laver, and the courtyard with its hangings — the outer elements of the sanctuary where sacrifice is made and the priests are washed. Then comes a careful accounting of all the gold, silver, and bronze used in the work. Every detail is recorded, every ounce of precious metal accounted for. This is stewardship and integrity in the service of God: the leaders give a transparent reckoning of the people's offerings.

One tender detail shines out: the bronze laver is made "from the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered at the entrance of the tent of meeting." The women give up their mirrors — instruments of self-regard and vanity in the ancient world — to be melted down into the basin where the priests wash to serve God. What a picture of consecration: surrendering the tools of self-focus to become instruments of cleansing for worship. As MacArthur observes, devotion to God transforms what we treasure, turning even our vanities into vessels of service.

The bronze altar at the entrance reminds us again that the way to God begins with sacrifice; the laver reminds us that those who draw near must be clean. And the meticulous accounting of materials teaches that the work of God is to be done with integrity and transparency, every gift faithfully stewarded. The same care God demanded in the design, his servants display in the reckoning — for all of it is done before the face of God, who sees and weighs every offering.

sections.title: The Bronze Altar and Laver
sections.commentary:
Bezalel makes the bronze altar of burnt offering with its horns, utensils, and grating, and the bronze laver. The altar stands at the entrance, where sacrifice is made; the laver provides water for the priests' cleansing. Together they declare the order of approach to God: first atonement (the altar), then cleansing (the laver), before entering his presence. There is no shortcut to God; the way runs through sacrifice and purification.

A tender detail shines out: the laver is made "from the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered in the entrance of the tent of meeting." The women surrender their bronze mirrors — instruments of self-regard in the ancient world — to be melted into the basin where priests wash for service. What a picture of consecration: the tools of vanity transformed into vessels of cleansing for worship. Devotion to God reorders what we treasure, turning even our self-focus into instruments of his service.

sections.title: The Court of the Tabernacle
sections.commentary:
Bezalel makes the courtyard with its hangings of fine twined linen on bronze-based pillars with silver hooks and fillets, and the screen for the gate woven in blue, purple, and scarlet. The court sets apart the sacred space and provides the one appointed entrance. All the pegs of the tabernacle and the court are of bronze. The boundary declares that God's dwelling is holy ground, entered only through the appointed way.

The single gate, beautifully woven, reminds us that there is one way into the presence of God — fulfilled in Christ, who declares, "I am the door" (John 10:9) and "I am the way" (John 14:6). The white linen surrounding the court speaks of the purity God requires, provided not by the worshiper's own righteousness but through the sacrifice within. Access to God is real, but on his terms, through his appointed means.

sections.title: The Reckoning of the Materials
sections.commentary:
The chapter ends with a careful accounting of all the gold, silver, and bronze used in the tabernacle, recorded "at the commandment of Moses" under the oversight of the Levites. Every talent and shekel is tallied. The silver comes from the atonement money, the half-shekel paid by each man counted in the census. The leaders give a transparent reckoning of the people's offerings, leaving no room for suspicion of mismanagement.

This meticulous accounting teaches that the work of God is to be done with integrity and transparency. Those entrusted with the people's gifts are accountable for every ounce. Paul echoes this principle in his careful handling of the collection for the saints, "taking precaution so that no one should blame us... for we aim at what is honorable not only in the Lord's sight but also in the sight of man" (2 Cor. 8:20-21). The same care God demanded in the design, his servants display in the reckoning — for all is done before the face of God who sees every gift.

sections.title: Atonement, Cleansing, and Integrity
sections.commentary:
The chapter holds together the order of approach to God (altar then laver — atonement then cleansing) and the integrity of God's work (every ounce of material accounted for). To draw near to God we must come through sacrifice and purification; to serve God we must handle his work with transparency and faithfulness.

The altar and laver point to Christ, through whose sacrifice and cleansing we approach the Father. The women's surrendered mirrors, melted into the laver, show how devotion to God transforms what we treasure. And the meticulous reckoning anticipates Paul's care with the saints' gifts, "aiming at what is honorable... in the sight of man" (2 Cor. 8:21). All our worship and service are done before the face of the God who sees.

38.theology:
The order of approach to God. The bronze altar (atonement) and laver (cleansing) at the entrance declare that we come to God through sacrifice and purification — fulfilled in Christ.

Consecration transforms what we treasure. The women give their mirrors to make the laver — devotion to God turns even the tools of vanity into instruments of his service.

Integrity in God's work. Every ounce of material is accounted for; the work of God is done with transparency and faithful stewardship (cf. 2 Cor. 8:20-21).
38.examples:
Then: Bezalel built the bronze altar and laver — made from the women's surrendered mirrors — and the court with its one appointed gate, and the leaders gave a careful, transparent reckoning of every gift the people had offered.

Now: We approach God only through sacrifice and cleansing, fulfilled in Christ, the one door and the one way. Devotion to God reorders our treasures, and the work of God is to be done with integrity and transparency — for all our giving and serving is done before the face of the God who sees.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-31 - The Bronze Altar, Basin, and Courtyard
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Construction of the bronze altar of burnt offering, the bronze basin for washing, and the courtyard with its linen curtains and bronze fittings. A tally of all the gold, silver, and bronze used in the tabernacle is given.
verseByVerse.theology: The accounting of materials — 29 talents and 730 shekels of gold, 100 talents and 1,775 shekels of silver, 70 talents and 2,400 shekels of bronze — is not bureaucratic record-keeping but theological testimony. Every ounce of material given by the people, freely and gladly, is accounted for before God and before the community. The stewardship of God's gifts requires accountability. The silver came from the atonement money — every adult Israelite's half-shekel ransom — reminding the community that the tabernacle stands on the foundation of redemption.
verseByVerse.examples: MacArthur notes that the bronze basin, made from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance to the tent of meeting, is one of the most touching details in the construction narrative. The women's mirrors — instruments of personal vanity — are melted into the basin for priestly washing. What served self-adornment now serves sacred cleansing. This is the shape of consecration.

verseByVerse.quote: The bronze altar: its grating of bronze, its poles, and all its utensils... He made the basin of bronze and its stand of bronze, from the mirrors of the ministering women who ministered in the entrance of the tent of meeting.
verseByVerse.commentary: The bronze altar — five cubits square, three cubits high, with its grating and poles — is where every sacrifice will be offered, every morning and evening, every Sabbath and feast day, year after year, generation after generation. It is built to last, overlaid with bronze, built for fire. The bronze basin for washing stands between the altar and the entrance to the Holy Place — before the priest can enter the presence of God, he must wash. The outer court defined by its linen curtains is 100 cubits by 50 cubits, one pillar and bronze peg after another, a visible boundary between the holy and the common. The whole tabernacle complex is a visual theology: come through the gate, pass the altar of sacrifice, wash at the basin, enter the Holy Place, approach the veil. This is the path of approach to God.

39.title: As the LORD Had Commanded Moses
39.text: <sup>32</sup>Thus all the work of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting was finished, and the people of Israel did according to all that the LORD had commanded Moses; so they did. <sup>42</sup>According to all that the LORD had commanded Moses, so the people of Israel had done all the work. <sup>43</sup>And Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it; as the LORD had commanded, so had they done it. Then Moses blessed them.
39.overview:
This chapter completes the priestly garments and brings the entire construction to its conclusion — and its dominant note is a refrain repeated like a drumbeat: "as the LORD had commanded Moses." Again and again, after each piece of work, the text says it was done exactly as the LORD commanded. The phrase appears seven times in this chapter, hammering home the theme of complete, faithful, joyful obedience. The people did all the work precisely according to God's word.

What a contrast to the golden calf! There, the people did exactly what they wanted; here, they do exactly what God commanded. The covenant broken by self-will is now honored by glad obedience. The repeated refrain is the language of a redeemed people delighting to do God's will — not grudgingly, but completely, down to the last detail. As Calvin noted, true worship consists not in human inventiveness but in conformity to God's revealed will.

And then the climactic scene: "Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it; as the LORD had commanded, so had they done it. Then Moses blessed them." The language deliberately echoes Genesis 1, where God "saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good," and then rested and blessed. The completion of the tabernacle is a kind of new creation — a finished work, inspected and blessed. As Christ would cry from the cross, "It is finished," so here the work of building God's dwelling is finished, and Moses pronounces blessing. The redeemed have built a home for God among them, exactly as he commanded, and it is good.

sections.title: The Priestly Garments Completed
sections.commentary:
The skilled workers make the priestly garments: the ephod of gold, blue, purple, and scarlet; the engraved onyx stones bearing Israel's names on the shoulder pieces; the breastpiece with its twelve precious stones; the robe with its bells and pomegranates; and the gold plate engraved "Holy to the LORD" for the turban. After each item, the refrain sounds: "as the LORD had commanded Moses." Every garment is made in precise obedience to God's design.

The garments that carry Israel's names on the high priest's shoulders and heart, and the plate declaring "Holy to the LORD," all point to Christ, our Great High Priest, who bears us into God's presence and is himself holy (Heb. 9:24). The careful, obedient crafting of these garments — "as the LORD had commanded" — declares that the way of mediation is appointed by God, not invented by man. We come to God only through the mediator he has provided, ultimately Christ himself.

sections.title: The Work Finished
sections.commentary:
"Thus all the work of the tabernacle of the tent of meeting was finished, and the people of Israel did according to all that the LORD had commanded Moses; so they did." The text then lists every completed component — the tent, the furnishings, the Ark, the table, the lampstand, the altars, the laver, the court, the garments — all brought to Moses. The refrain "as the LORD had commanded Moses" sounds again and again, a drumbeat of faithful obedience.

What a contrast to the golden calf, where the people did exactly as they pleased! Here they do exactly as God commanded, down to the last detail. The covenant broken by self-will is honored by glad obedience. The repeated refrain is the language of a redeemed people delighting to do God's will completely. This is the fruit of grace: not grudging compliance but joyful, thorough conformity to the will of the God who saved them.

sections.title: Moses Inspects and Blesses
sections.commentary:
The chapter reaches its climax: "According to all that the LORD had commanded Moses, so the people of Israel had done all the work. And Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it; as the LORD had commanded, so had they done it. Then Moses blessed them." The language deliberately echoes the creation account, where God "saw everything that he had made, and behold, it was very good," then rested and blessed.

The completion of the tabernacle is presented as a kind of new creation — a finished work, inspected and pronounced good, and crowned with blessing. As Christ would one day cry from the cross, "It is finished," so here the work of building God's dwelling is complete. The redeemed have, in obedience to God's word, built a home for God among them, and Moses blesses them. The God who created the world to dwell with man, and who redeemed a people to dwell among them, now has a dwelling prepared — pointing forward to the day when, in Christ, the dwelling of God is with man forever (Rev. 21:3).

sections.title: Glad Obedience as Worship
sections.commentary:
The drumbeat refrain of the chapter — "as the LORD had commanded Moses," sounded again and again — is the language of glad, complete obedience. What a reversal from the golden calf, where the people did exactly as they pleased! Here a redeemed people delight to do God's will down to the last detail. Obedience is not the enemy of grace but its fruit.

And the closing scene echoes creation: Moses sees the finished work, finds it done as commanded, and blesses the people — as God saw his creation "very good," then blessed and rested. The completion of God's dwelling is a new-creation moment, anticipating the greater finished work of Christ, who cried "It is finished," that God might dwell with his people forever.

39.theology:
Complete, joyful obedience. The refrain "as the LORD had commanded Moses" sounds throughout — the redeemed delight to do God's will completely, in contrast to the self-will of the golden calf.

Worship by God's design. Both the priestly garments and the structure are made exactly as commanded; the way of mediation and worship is appointed by God, fulfilled in Christ.

A finished work, inspected and blessed. The completion echoes creation — Moses sees, it is done as commanded, and he blesses, anticipating Christ's "It is finished."
39.examples:
Then: The priestly garments and the whole tabernacle were completed exactly "as the LORD had commanded Moses," and Moses inspected the finished work, saw it was done as commanded, and blessed the people — a new-creation scene of faithful obedience.

Now: Grace produces glad, complete obedience — not the self-will of the golden calf but the joyful conformity of a redeemed people to God's will. The finished tabernacle, inspected and blessed, points to the greater finished work of Christ, who cried "It is finished" so that God might dwell with us forever.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The craftsmen make the priestly garments exactly as God commanded: the ephod of gold and colored yarns, the breastpiece with its twelve precious stones, the robe of the ephod with its pomegranates and golden bells, the tunics, turbans, and the golden plate. Moses inspects the work and blesses the people.
verseByVerse.theology: The completion of the priestly garments is narrated with the refrain as the LORD had commanded Moses appearing seven times in this chapter. Seven times — the number of completion. The obedience is total and joyful. The final act is Moses inspecting the work and seeing that they had done it as the LORD had commanded. Then he blessed them. This is the approval of God through his servant: the work done faithfully receives blessing.
verseByVerse.examples: Begg observes that the twelve stones of the breastpiece — sardius, topaz, carbuncle; emerald, sapphire, diamond; jacinth, agate, amethyst; beryl, onyx, jasper — represent the twelve tribes, each stone a different gem, each gem engraved with a name. Every tribe has its own gem. The diversity of the community is honored by the diversity of the jewels. No two tribes are identical; all are precious; all are carried on the high priest's heart.

verseByVerse.quote: According to all that the LORD had commanded Moses, so the people of Israel had done all the work. And Moses saw all the work, and behold, they had done it; as the LORD had commanded, so had they done it. Then Moses blessed them.
verseByVerse.commentary: The construction narrative ends in blessing. Moses inspects every element — the tabernacle, the tent, the ark, the mercy seat, the table, the lampstand, the altar of incense, the anointing oil, the fragrant incense, the screen for the entrance to the tent, the bronze altar, the bronze basin, the courtyard, the garments, the plate — and sees that every piece has been made exactly as the LORD commanded.
