The repeated refrain as the LORD had commanded Moses is the theological verdict on the entire construction project: it is faithful. And faithful work receives blessing. This is the pattern of covenant obedience: hear, do, receive blessing. The blessing of Moses over the completed work of God's people is a small anticipation of the great blessing: well done, good and faithful servant.

40.title: The Glory of the LORD Filled the Tabernacle
40.text: <sup>34</sup>Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. <sup>35</sup>And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. <sup>38</sup>For the cloud of the LORD was on the tabernacle by day, and fire was in it by night, in the sight of all the house of Israel throughout all their journeys.
40.overview:
The book of Exodus reaches its glorious climax. The tabernacle is erected, exactly as God commanded, on the first day of the first month — a new beginning, a new year, a new creation. Moses sets up every piece in its appointed place: the Ark behind the veil, the table and lampstand and altar of incense in the Holy Place, the bronze altar and laver in the court. And once more the refrain sounds, "as the LORD had commanded Moses," seven times over. The dwelling place of God among his people is ready.

And then — the climax of the entire book: "the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle." The Shekinah glory, the visible presence of God, descends and fills the tent so fully that even Moses cannot enter. The God who came down to deliver his people from Egypt has now come down to dwell among them. The book that began with a people enslaved in a foreign land ends with God himself dwelling in their midst, leading them by cloud and fire through all their journeys. The whole movement of Exodus has been toward this moment: God with his people.

And this is only the beginning of the story. The glory that filled the tabernacle would one day fill the incarnate Christ, in whom "the Word became flesh and dwelt [tabernacled] among us, and we have seen his glory" (John 1:14). At Pentecost the glory would fill the temple of the church by the Spirit. And in the end, the glory will fill the New Jerusalem, where "the dwelling place of God is with man," and there will be no temple, "for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb" (Rev. 21:3, 22). The God who redeems is the God who dwells with us — now and forevermore.

sections.title: The Tabernacle Erected
sections.commentary:
God commands Moses to set up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month — a new beginning, like a new creation. Moses is to place the Ark behind the veil, set up the table and lampstand and altar of incense, position the bronze altar and laver, erect the court, and anoint the tabernacle and the priests, consecrating them for service. Everything is to be ordered exactly as God directs, each object in its appointed place.

The first day of the first month signals a fresh start: God is establishing his dwelling among his people as the inauguration of a new era. The careful ordering and anointing of every element, and the consecration of the priests, prepares the way for God's glory to descend. All is made ready for the holy God to take up residence among his redeemed people — the goal toward which the entire book has been moving.

sections.title: Moses Obeys in Every Detail
sections.commentary:
Moses does everything "as the LORD had commanded him" — the refrain sounds seven times in this section as each element is set in place: the frames, the Ark and the testimony, the veil, the table and its bread, the lampstand and its lamps, the golden altar of incense, the screen, the bronze altar with its offerings, the laver for washing, and the court. "So Moses finished the work." The completion echoes both creation ("God finished his work") and anticipates Christ's "It is finished."

The relentless repetition of "as the LORD had commanded" crowns the book's theme of joyful, complete obedience. From the broken covenant of the golden calf, God has brought his people to faithful conformity to his will. The dwelling of God is prepared not by human creativity but by humble obedience to God's revealed word. Moses finishes the work, and all stands ready for the glory to descend. The pattern of a finished work preparing for God's presence points to the finished work of Christ that opens the way into God's eternal presence.

sections.title: The Glory Fills the Tabernacle
sections.commentary:
Then comes the climax of the entire book: "the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle." The Shekinah glory, the visible presence of God, descends and fills the tent so fully that even Moses cannot enter. The God who came down to deliver his people now comes down to dwell among them.

The book that began with a people enslaved in a foreign land ends with God himself dwelling in their midst, leading them by cloud by day and fire by night through all their journeys. This is the goal toward which all of Exodus has moved: God with his people. And it is only the beginning. The glory that filled the tabernacle would one day fill the incarnate Christ, in whom "the Word became flesh and dwelt [tabernacled] among us, and we have seen his glory" (John 1:14). At Pentecost the glory filled the temple of the church by the Spirit. And in the end, the glory will fill the New Jerusalem, where "the dwelling place of God is with man," and there is no temple, "for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb" (Rev. 21:3, 22). The God who redeems is the God who dwells with us — now and forevermore. To this end he brought us out; to this end he brought us in: that he might be our God, and we his people, dwelling in his glorious presence forever.

sections.title: The Goal of the Whole Book: God With Us
sections.commentary:
The final scene is the goal toward which the entire book has moved: "the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle." The book that opened with a people enslaved in a foreign land closes with God himself dwelling in their midst, leading them by cloud and fire through all their journeys. From bondage to glory, from groaning to the Shekinah presence — this is the arc of redemption.

And it is only the beginning. The glory that filled the tabernacle filled the incarnate Christ, in whom "the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory" (John 1:14); it filled the church at Pentecost by the Spirit; and it will fill the New Jerusalem, where "the dwelling place of God is with man," with no temple, "for its temple is the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb" (Rev. 21:3, 22). The God who redeems is the God who dwells with us — now and forevermore. He brought us out that he might bring us in.

40.theology:
God dwells with his people. The glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle — the climax of Exodus. The God who came down to deliver comes down to dwell. "I will dwell among them" is fulfilled.

A finished work and a new creation. "Moses finished the work" on the first day of the first month echoes creation and points to Christ's finished work that opens the way into God's presence.

The trajectory of glory. The tabernacle glory points to Christ who tabernacled among us (John 1:14), to Pentecost, and finally to the New Jerusalem where God dwells with man forever (Rev. 21:3).
40.examples:
Then: Moses erected the tabernacle exactly as God commanded, and the glory of the LORD descended and filled it so fully that even Moses could not enter. The God who redeemed his people from Egypt now dwelt in their midst, leading them by cloud and fire.

Now: The whole book has moved toward this: God with his people. The glory that filled the tabernacle filled the incarnate Christ, fills the church by the Spirit, and will fill the New Jerusalem forever. The God who redeems is the God who dwells with us. He brought us out that he might bring us in — to dwell in his glorious presence, our God forever, world without end.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1-38 - The Tabernacle Erected and the Glory Fills It
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God commands Moses to set up the tabernacle on the first day of the first month. Moses does so, anointing and consecrating every element. When everything is in place, the cloud covers the tent of meeting and the glory of the LORD fills the tabernacle. Moses cannot enter because of the glory.
verseByVerse.theology: The final scene of Exodus is the most magnificent in the book: the glory of the LORD filling the tabernacle, the cloud settling on it by day, the fire in it by night. God moves in. The whole book has been building to this moment — liberation from Egypt so that God might dwell with his people. And now he does. Moses cannot enter because the glory is too great. The book ends not with a law or a command but with the presence of God — the cloud and fire that will lead Israel through the wilderness to the Promised Land.
verseByVerse.examples: Ferguson writes that the final verse of Exodus — throughout all their journeys, whenever the cloud was taken up from over the tabernacle, the people of Israel would set out. But if the cloud was not taken up, then they did not set out till the day that it was lifted — is the picture of the Christian life: not moving by our own plans or schedules, but going where the presence of God leads, staying where he rests.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle.
verseByVerse.commentary: The dedication of the tabernacle is accomplished not by a ceremony or a sacrifice but by the arrival of God himself. Moses has done everything exactly as the LORD commanded — the refrain runs seven more times through this chapter — and when the last piece is in place, the cloud descends and the glory fills the house. The same cloud that led Israel through the wilderness, that stood between Israel and the Egyptian army at the sea, that settled on Sinai — now settles on the tabernacle. God is home. He dwells among his people. The whole story of the Bible is the story of God seeking to dwell with his people, from the garden of Eden to the New Jerusalem where the dwelling of God is with man and he will dwell with them and they will be his people and he will be their God. Exodus has brought us one step closer to that final fulfillment.
